utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: We should deal first with the motion raised at the end of yesterday's proceedings. Disclosure to the Defence is sought of the record of an interview conducted by the Prosecutor with Agim Murtezi. As the submission was developed, it also extended to other materials. But no distinct basis is suggested on which those further materials ought to be provided, other than that which is the one primarily addressed to the record of an interview. So they, all materials, may be adequately considered in the context of the primary submission. Now, Murtezi was originally charged with the three present accused. After his arrest, he was interviewed. We are informed that following the interview the Prosecutor was able to confirm his account that he was not at Lapusnik at the time charged. The Prosecutor accepted there had been a mistake in identification of Murtezi, and did not proceed further against him. Rule 68, which is relied on in support of the motion, obliges disclosure by the Prosecutor of material which may suggest innocence or mitigate the guilt of or affect the credibility of Prosecution evidence against the accused. Counsel for the Prosecutor assures the Chamber that there has been no failure to comply with the Rule. The jurisprudence of the Tribunal confirms that this obligation to comply with Rule 68 in good faith lies on the Prosecutor. The Chamber will not intervene in the absence of some demonstrated basis for the view that the Prosecutor has failed to discharge this obligation. In this respect, we would simply refer by way of example to decisions in Brdjanin, Delalic, and the Appeals Chamber decision in Blaskic. It was not the case, as was put in reply, that the Defence should be allowed to view the materials to satisfy themselves that Rule 68 has been complied with. Issues of identification will be alive in this trial in respect of each of the three accused. It is not apparent, however, that an error of identification affecting Murtezi will bear on the identification of any of the other accused or will otherwise be relevant to their cases. Of course there could be some connection, but nothing is before the Chamber to suggest that this is such a case. The circumstances do not indicate to the Chamber, as is submitted, that the whole investigative process is called into question by virtue of a mistaken identification. In the view of the Chamber, therefore, no basis is advanced on which the Chamber should not accept the assurance of counsel for the Prosecution. An issue such as this ought to have been resolved at the pre-trial stage. The only justification for it being raised at this stage is the second basis upon which the motion was supported. The interview by the Prosecutor with Murtezi was mentioned in the course of the opening by counsel for the Prosecution. It is submitted that thereby the interview with Murtezi became part of the Prosecution case, and as such should be disclosed. This is more a Rule 66 issue than Rule 68. However, no more was said in opening than to offer a brief explanation why the present proceedings are only against the three present accused rather than four, as originally charged. It is not proposed by the Prosecution to call Murtezi; what was said in opening did not suggest otherwise. In the Chamber's view, the mention in opening provides no basis for a disclosure order at this stage. It was also ventured in reply that the Defence may wish to call Murtezi. That possibility does not provide a basis upon which disclosure should be ordered. The motion is therefore dismissed. Now, Mr. Whiting or Mr. Cayley, I've lost track of which, the question of the witness subject to protective measures, you were going to reflect overnight on some views that were advanced for your consideration. Could you do so now.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. We did reflect, and I believe that the course set out by Your Honours is one that makes sense, one that we will follow. Of course, it -- my intention was not simply to protect the name but to protect the name in connection with information that was subsequently elicited. However, on further careful reflection, I think the information that was elicited is not unique to that individual. Therefore, I don't think in this case -- in this instance there's any problem with releasing the name. I don't know if the Court would like to simply enter an order to unseal, as it were, that portion of the transcript. Or if you would prefer that we -- I put the question in open session today and repeat that question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER

Had you given thought to that?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER

utterances.speaker: OLE LEHTINEN [Resumed]

Worked against crime including criminal investigations against drug traffic "Wishes to have career as criminal investigator."

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Could you read now please what is written after "social conduct" on that page, what's highlighted, please.

utterances.speaker: OLE LEHTINEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: "Social conduct: Involved in Karate."

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: And finally on that page the portions that's highlighted on that screen.

utterances.speaker: OLE LEHTINEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: "Acceptance of rules: Would enforce the law strictly and equally. Might bend the law in certain situations."

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: If you could turn now please to the page marked 6276. This is an observation report from Mr. Musliu for in-service training programme from the 3rd to the 7th of September in 2001. I would ask you to turn to the second page of that document, 6277, and read what's highlighted on the screen, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOPOLSKI
utterances.text: Your Honours, forgive me, before the witness responds. utterances.speaker: MR. TOPOLSKI

utterances.speaker: MR. TOPOLSKI

utterances.speaker: OLE LEHTINEN [Resumed]

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Turning now --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated].

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Mr. Lehtinen, was Mr. Musliu interviewed in connection with this investigation?

utterances.speaker: OLE LEHTINEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: On what date?

utterances.speaker: OLE LEHTINEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: There was an interview with Mr. Musliu on 24th of May, 2001.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: And did that predate the involvement of the ICTY in the investigation?

utterances.speaker: OLE LEHTINEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: So who conducted the interview?

utterances.speaker: OLE LEHTINEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: This interview was conducted by an investigator with the so-called CCIU in the UNMIK police in Pristina.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Could you tell the Court, please, what CCIU stands for.

utterances.speaker: OLE LEHTINEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: CCIU sign language an abbreviation for Central Criminal Investigations Unit.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: And they are a part of UNMIK, which is the civilian administration in Kosovo?

utterances.speaker: OLE LEHTINEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Have you had occasion to speak with Mr. Berkolin [phoen], who has conducted in interview?

utterances.speaker: OLE LEHTINEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I have.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Has he confirmed that the record of the interview which is at 03231634 to 1635 is accurate?

utterances.speaker: OLE LEHTINEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, he has confirmed that.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: I would ask you please to read the section that's highlighted on the screen.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: And if Mr. Younis could blow it up, please.

utterances.speaker: OLE LEHTINEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: "On March 1998 I came back from Germany, where I had been a refugee. The same month I started to serve as a UCK soldier in Drenica valley. I served as a soldier for about six weeks and then became a team leader in Lapusnik area. In my team I had in the beginning 11 soldiers and at the most 15 to 16 members. In August 1998 became a deputy commander of UCK Brigade 121 in Narradin [sic] fighting area. Narradin fighting area included the municipalities of Lipjan, Shtime, Ferizaj, and Kachanik. Then in December 1998 I became the commander of the UCK military police in the Narradin area. I had this position until KFOR entered Kosovo, June 1999.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: According to the record of the interview, was Mr. Musliu asked about a series of persons who had been abducted?

utterances.speaker: OLE LEHTINEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: If you could just read through the names there of the persons who he was asked about.

utterances.speaker: OLE LEHTINEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's Ademi, Agim; Vesiqi, Rahim; Xhemshiti, Lutfi; Berbatovci, Ismail; Hoxha, Hasan.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: And on the following page.

utterances.speaker: OLE LEHTINEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's Ahmeti, Vesel; Bajrami, Imri; Zymeri, Shyqyri; Rexhaj, Hetem.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Is it fair to say that with respect to all the persons, he said he knew nothing about their disappearance?

utterances.speaker: OLE LEHTINEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: With respect to the last person, Mr. Hetem Rexhaj, he provided additional information. What did he say?

utterances.speaker: OLE LEHTINEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'll read again from the screen. He said, "I knew this person from before the war but I don't know anything about his disappearance."

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Subsequently he was asked some questions about Lapusnik. Could you read the two questions and answers which follow on the record of the interview.

utterances.speaker: OLE LEHTINEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. The first question is: "The summer 1998 you was a team leader in the Lapusnik area. Do you know anything about a house/outhouse used as a prison in this area?" And the answer is: "Lapusnik fighting area was divided in 3 to 4 parts. I was serving in one of them. In my area, there were no prisons and I have not heard about any prisons." The second question: "A prison in Lapusnik area had a commander called Haradin Balay [sic], nicknamed Shala. Another soldier in this prison was Agim Murtezi nicknamed Murizzi. A witness also stated that you visited this prison every 3 to 4 days?" The answer is: "I had two persons in my team with the nickname Shala. I don't know if any of them was Haradin Bala. Agim Murtezi or Murizzi I have never heard about. I have never visited any prison in the Lapusnik area."

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Your Honour, could this exhibit be given a number, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That will be Prosecution Exhibit P32.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Turning now to tab 27, which is 03231639 to 1641. Was Mr. Musliu also interviewed in connection with another investigation that day?

utterances.speaker: OLE LEHTINEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: And is this the record of the interview?

utterances.speaker: OLE LEHTINEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: This appearance to be the record of the interview. I have not spoken to this investigator.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Now, with respect to this interview and the preceding interview, does the Albanian version of the record of the interview contain Mr. Musliu's signature?

utterances.speaker: OLE LEHTINEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: And how do you know it is his signature?

utterances.speaker: OLE LEHTINEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have compared the signature of these statements with the signatures in Mr. Musliu's personal file, and they appear to be the same.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Now, with respect to this second interview conducted on the same day, I would ask if you could to read the highlighted portion on the first page.

utterances.speaker: OLE LEHTINEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: "Before March 1998 I was a refugee in Germany. In March 1998 I came back to Kosovo and was a KLA soldier for roughly 4 to 6 weeks only. Then I was a team leader of a fighting KLA group for approximately 3 or 3 and a half months in the area of Lapusnik until summer 1998. "Then I became deputy commander of KLA Brigade 121. After that I changed to the KLA military police, I think in December 1998."

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: If you could turn to the next page and read the highlighted portion on that page, please.

utterances.speaker: OLE LEHTINEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: "It is possible that some persons/KLA members have been arrested during the war because of cooperating with the Serbs. But these people were not arrested like real prisoners as far as I know. "They have been kept I would say. We had no KLA prisons or detention centres. I know nothing about that. In that time we even had good contact to the people working for the OSCE. These people came sometimes to look after the arrested/kept people. "During war I had nothing to do with arrested people. I gave no orders concerning that. In the first part of the war, it was my job to fight against the enemy and at the front line. And as the leader of the military police in the Nerodimlje area, I also had nothing to do with arresting people. In my area, we had no prisons or something like that. "I can tell you that I really know nothing about missing persons. Perhaps these missing people cooperated with the Serbs in former times. I don't know. "We all know also what is blood revenge is. That can also be a motivation for people calling my name in some cases or telling lies about me. I gave no orders to kidnap or kill anybody. Some people are misusing my name. They are telling lies about my person. A lot of people even don't know my real name. A lot of people know my nickname. A lot of people in Kosovo know my nickname. That is sure."

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Your Honour, I would ask that this be given a number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That will be Prosecution Exhibit P33.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Your Honours, I also just noticed on my screen that the -- if it's set to computer evidence as opposed to video evidence the documents are much clearer. I don't know if that's been a problem for others.

utterances.text: Thank you very much for that.

utterances.text: Turning now to the video marked V0004095 and the corresponding transcript, which is at tab 28.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Mr. Lehtinen, how was this documentary obtained?

utterances.speaker: OLE LEHTINEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: This documentary we received information that this documentary was existing in the RTK, which is a television company in Kosovo, and by request we received a copy of it from this television company.

utterances.text: What is the documentary about?

utterances.text: This is about the KLA forming itself in the area of Klecka and the Berisa mountains. And it centres around a person, a martyr, called Sadik Shala and his experiences with the KLA.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: And what time period is covered by the documentary?

utterances.speaker: OLE LEHTINEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's mostly the spring and the first part of summer of 1998.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: And Sadik Shala, when was he killed?

utterances.speaker: OLE LEHTINEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sadik Shala died around the 20th of July, 1998.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Who are some of the people who appear in the video or who are mentioned?

utterances.speaker: OLE LEHTINEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: There's interviews with former KLA soldiers. Mr. Fatmir Limaj is interviewed. Haxhi Shala, Mr. Shukri Buja and then members of the family of the martyr Sadik Shala.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Your Honours, I'm going to show a series of clips and have each one introduced by Mr. Lehtinen. The transcript of the clips will be synchronised with the video that's shown. The first clip is from pages 1 through 3 of the transcript.

utterances.text: Yes. This clip describes how the Kosovo Liberation Army started its formation in the Berisa mountains. utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Could we see the clip, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: The second clip appears on page 4 of the transcript. Could you briefly introduce that clip, please.

utterances.speaker: OLE LEHTINEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, the following clip describes Sadik Shala and his involvement in the 121st Brigade in the Pashtrik Operation Zone and also his involvement in the formation of the Celiku unit.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Could we see that clip, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: The third clip is on page 6 of the transcript.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: And what is that clip about, please?

utterances.speaker: OLE LEHTINEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: This clip -- in this clip, Mr. Fatmir Limaj describes Sadik Shala as being one of the first persons to enter the books of the 121st Brigade. And he also describes an event in March of 1998 when KLA soldiers enter Stimlje in uniforms.

utterances.speaker: OLE LEHTINEN [Resumed]

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Could we see this next clip, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: The next clip is on page 7.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: The next clip is the second half of page 11.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING

utterances.speaker: OLE LEHTINEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: This clip is about the fighting in the town of Rahovec starting on the 17th of July, 1998, describing the Celiku soldiers of the 121st Brigade and Sadik Shala taking part in this.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Could we see this clip, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Mr. Lehtinen, could you describe for the Court where Rahovec is, please.

utterances.speaker: OLE LEHTINEN [Resumed]

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: If we -- if you could put map 5 on the ELMO, please.

utterances.speaker: OLE LEHTINEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Map 5 you said?

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: I don't believe it's on map 6.

utterances.speaker: OLE LEHTINEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: And if we could switch to the ELMO. And now I think we have to switch to video evidence to get that.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Could you circle Rahovec, please, on that map.

utterances.speaker: OLE LEHTINEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Witness complies]

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: If now we could switch back to the Sanction. The next clip starts on page 12.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Could you introduce that clip please for the Court.

utterances.speaker: OLE LEHTINEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is a man called Habib Murina talking again about the fighting in Rahovec. In this clip when he talks about Fatmir Limaj, he calls him by the pseudonym of Daja, meaning uncle.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Could we see this clip, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Finally, the last clip from this documentary is on page -- starts on page 14.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING

utterances.speaker: OLE LEHTINEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Again, it's a continuation of the -- what happened in Rahovec and the death of Sadik Shala and how Commander Limaj ordered the soldiers to bury him in the prison graveyard. And Limaj also talks about other losses of the 121st Brigade in this fight.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Could we see this clip, please.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: [Voiceover] ... to get the lifeless bodies of the martyrs that were killed in the fighting in the city, near the Rahovec waterworks. Beqir Hoxha: When we came here we started to bring out Sadik's body, Sadik Shala's, and so then, start the guard, the graveyard guards had noticed that someone was doing something there, and so we weren't successful on the first night and the Shkjas noticed also and came with some armoured vehicles, and with their vehicles so we opened fire on them so there was no success on the first night. We came again two nights later and with Commander Remzi Ademaj, he helped us and also offered...

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: There seems to be a problem with the transmission.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: I haven't yet grasped what the problem is. Does it still exist?

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Well, it's -- okay.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: I'm getting indications that it has resolved.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: If we could continue with the clip.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: [Voiceover] ... He offered us munitions and with the help of those soldiers and our comrades we got the body and we it there to Klecka where this place was and Sadik Shala was buried in Klecka with military honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: I'm told we are getting English language on the Albanian-language channel sometimes. Thank you.

utterances.text: Continue please.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Turning now, please, to the document following tab 29. And the Prosecution will -- this is another videotape, V0004733, and the corresponding transcript. And again, Your Honour, I would ask that both be numbered.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: The video will be exhibit -- Prosecution Exhibit P35 and the corresponding transcript P35.1.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Mr. Lehtinen, this is a documentary. When was it made?

utterances.speaker: OLE LEHTINEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: This documentary about Fatmir Limaj seems to have been made after his arrest by the ICTY.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: How was it obtained?

utterances.speaker: OLE LEHTINEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not quite sure how this was obtained, but it was shown on local TV in Kosovo after the arrest of Mr. Limaj.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: I'm going to show two clips from this video. The first clip begins on page 1 and runs for two pages.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Could you introduce this clip, please.

utterances.speaker: OLE LEHTINEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. In this first clip Fatmir Limaj is described as a person and is the commander of the 121st Brigade and a member of the General Staff. There's footage of -- again of the same oath ceremony that we saw earlier. And later there's footage from a meeting between KLA soldiers and representatives, diplomats of the United States and Europe in a place called Dragobilje.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Now, in the previous documentary when the oath ceremony was shown there was a date -- it said June 1998, on the screen. When this -- when the same oath ceremony is shown in this video, is the date included on the screen?

utterances.speaker: OLE LEHTINEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: There's no date on this footage.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Could we see this clip, please.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: [Voiceover] Fatmir Limaj, known as Commander Celiku, is one of the central figures of the KLA who led the armed resistance of the people of Kosova against the militarist regime of Belgrade. He was born on the 4th of February, 1971, in Banje near Malisheva. He is a law graduate and did his postgraduate studies in international relations at the Law Faculty of Pristina University. During the war for the liberation of Kosova from the Serb occupation forces, Fatmir Limaj was commander of the 121st Brigade and member of the General Staff of the KLA. Let us go on to watch some documentary film that shows Fatmir Limaj at the same time as a fighter for freedom and a fighter for peace. As a member of the Kosovo Liberation Army. Soldiers: As a member of the KLA. I swear that I will always be a loyal soldier, a worthy fighter for freedom, vigilant, courageous and disciplined, ready at any time, not sparing my own life, to fight, to defend the sacred interests of the homeland. This is how Fatmir Limaj explained the decision of the SVA to the KLA to base itself in the mountains of Berisha, that is in Klecka, and Divjake. ... considering the terrain and the local population, the SHP, the General Staffof the KLA decided that Klecka would -- too would become one of its important bases. Our national movement.... as it is well known... these mountains have been famous in the past, and national movements for the liberation of Kosova have sent people to this area at different times and they have found shelter and powerful support from the local population. In the eighties too, these mountains were in one way or another a strength and stay for the underground movements of distinguished activists, most of whom has now been killed. For instance, the mountains for Berisha whilst the home of Afrim Zhitia and Fadil Varta and others. In short, there is a continuity to these mountains, which have always sheltered those who have worked and taken action for the freedom of Kosova. So, of course we had a safe place here, we knew that the population would support us, and in practice it was not hard for the KLA to establish itself here and to create one of its most powerful bases. Fatmir Limaj was always with the political representatives of the KLA in talks that were held with representatives of the United Stated and European diplomacy. One must single out especially the meetings that took place at Dragobil near Malisheva.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Could you pause it here.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: There's a date that appears on this portion of the clip. Do you know -- it's in Albanian, but do you know what that date is?

utterances.speaker: OLE LEHTINEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. That's the 6th of November, 1998.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: And who is that person who i son the screen at the moment?

utterances.speaker: OLE LEHTINEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is Mr. Hashim Thaqi.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Thank you. Could you finish.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: The second clip -- this transcript unfortunately doesn't -- the pages are not numbered. So it's three, four, five -- page eight, counting in to page 8. The top of the page is "FL: When the international community."

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Could you introduce this brief clip, please. The Court has already seen it. So could you introduce it.

utterances.speaker: OLE LEHTINEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is Fatmir Limaj speaking to the soldiers. It's dated May 1999 and he talks about being a fanatic for order and discipline.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Could we see this clip, please.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: [Voiceover] You know that in all the armies of the world, and in our liberation army too, order and discipline are an essential condition for our success. Just to tell you in brief, I inform you that I am a fanatic for order and discipline, and I will not permit any soldier or officer to violate the KLA's order and discipline. Self-denial, struggle, and morale are conditions for the success of a KLA freedom fighter. I am convinced that it is the blood of our sons, the blood of our youngest, most dedicated, and finest sons that brought this success. Nobody else brought it to us. It was the struggle of the KLA that brought the Albanian people to the international position they are in.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Turning now to the next document after tab 30. And this is another documentary video, V0002527. Again, I would ask that the video and the corresponding transcript which is here be given numbers.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: The video will be Prosecution Exhibit P36 and the corresponding transcript P36.1.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Mr. Lehtinen, what is this documentary, or rather what is this video?

utterances.speaker: OLE LEHTINEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is a television interview with Mr. Fatmir Limaj. It's done by the United Kingdom's Channel 4 News.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: And do you know when the interview was done?

utterances.speaker: OLE LEHTINEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not sure. It's clearly after the war, and the tape with the interview is dated on the 18th of August, 2000.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: The first clip that I'm going to show is on page 1. Could you introduce that clip, please, to the Court.

utterances.speaker: OLE LEHTINEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Limaj is asked about why the Kosovars began their armed uprising, and Mr. Limaj explains that this was a result of the failed policy -- politics of Mr. Ibrahim Rugova and that they thought the only way to work it -- to work for a decision of the Albanians in Kosovo is an armed uprising.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Who is Mr. Rugova?

utterances.speaker: OLE LEHTINEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Ibrahim Rugova is the leader of the LDK party, which is the Democratic League of Kosovo.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: And was he in that position during the war?

utterances.speaker: OLE LEHTINEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Can we see this clip, please.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: [Voiceover] why did the Kosovars start an armed uprising? The Kosovars started an armed uprising after losing all their hopes. In that -- our way of achieving our national goal had failed. In particular, the so-called peaceful pacifists road under the leadership of Rugova failed. And the Albanians were finally persuaded that to achieve their national interests, they had to shift to armed resistance, as other people had done. There was a widespread view among the people, whereas some people had already started preparations for the armed resistance that would later be identified with the Kosovo Liberation Army. It was clear to them that our national interests could only be realised through armed resistance. After all other options had been exhausted, after the constant occupation and the incessant repression of the Serb -- Serbian regime. Even though the Albanians behaved in a civilised manner and asked for and articulated their demands in a peaceful way and had given up the street protests that had previously been one of the main ways in which our people had demonstrated their discontent. They had sacrifices, that is these gave up even those popular protests and took to office work, conferences, resolutions, protests. How shall I put it? By organising a sort of literary discussions, expressing their opposition to violence. Nevertheless, the Serb state responded in the harshest way to this behaviour of the Albanian people and the political class. Seeing that there was no other way and there was no talking with the Milosevic regime and seeing this manner of realising our national interests could absolutely not get through in the case of Milosevic, they moved to the armed resistance, which I have said before, as been identified with the KLA.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: The next clip is on page 2 of the transcript.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Could you introduce that, please.

utterances.speaker: OLE LEHTINEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yeah. The interview continues on the same topic. And Mr. Limaj describes the years from 1993 to 1996 as being the period when people who were against the politics of Rugova emerged and started to form what would become the Kosovo Liberation Army.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Could we see this clip, please.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: [Voiceover] It was precisely seeing that, as I said earlier, all the other options and that the people were in a way fed up with these kinds of resistance and that a kind of mood had arisen among Albanian youth to look for other kinds of action. This was first expressed among some political parties, organisations, and you could see that people in Kosovo were thinking of other alternatives, that is in a word in 1996 and especially from 1993 to 1996, those who did not support Rugova's peaceful road, that is in that simple sense began to make themselves felt. So this sense some people were prepared to take this path, that is an alternative to the peaceful road and created the KLA. I think that in this aspect, how shall I put it, there were three main aspects to the conditions for the creation of the KLA. First, the Albanians of Kosovo had all the conditions with the economic potential to wage a war. Secondly, they had the political potential to justify that war. And thirdly, they had the strength, the sufficient physique -- physical strength to wage the war. I am talking specifically here. And we know that there was a great part of the young people are young and always ready at any time to make sacrifices. They are always ready and their strength only needs to be mobilised.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: The third clip is on page 5.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Could you introduce that clip, please.

utterances.speaker: OLE LEHTINEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. In this part Mr. Limaj is asked about his personal role as a KLA member, and he describes himself as part of the leadership of KLA.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Could we see this clip, please.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: [Voiceover] How did you assess your personal role as a member of the KLA? I think that my role, like that of all other members of the KLA, was to use all our intellectual and physical resources and to be ready to sacrifice ourselves for the great cause. I think that it was what every Albanian in this country had to be ready to do. Considering the group of young men they took up, you, Hashim ^ , and the others, how do you assess the role of this section of the KLA leadership? What role did they really have? I think that these people had a two-fold role, both waging the war and justifying the war -- or rather, carrying out the politics of the war and taking direct part in the war and in extending and organising the KLA. Am I right in saying that this group of people were in fact the real leadership of the KLA from the beginning? Of course, of course. Can you say all of them? This entire group in the beginning down to the present day has been the real leadership of the KLA. And indeed at the time it was a two-fold leadership. Now it is a political leadership, but then afs also military leadership that worked on and prepared the strategy of military action and with all the resources it possessed. It extended in the organisational sense. The units of the KLA throughout Kosovo. It was involved in border crossings, supplies, caring for our comrades' families, everything. So it was this group.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Your Honour, I note the time. I don't believe I'll be able to finish this exhibit. It will take another five or ten minutes. Perhaps --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Very well. Thank you, Mr. Whiting. We will adjourn now until 4.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Whiting, I was not yet --

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Yes, I can say something?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Whiting.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Your Honour, before I proceed Mr. Cayley had to step out to attend to a matter. He asked to be excused.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Mr. Lehtinen, we were going through this documentary and we're going to move to the next clip which starts on page 6 of the transcript, and again, this is at tab 30. Could you please introduce this next clip.

utterances.speaker: OLE LEHTINEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. In this part of the interview, Mr. Limaj is asked to describe some incidents. He describes one in the year of 1996 when there was a lot of secrecy around the KLA. And then he proceeds to describe an incident on the 26th of November, 1997, in Ljudevic which is important date and incident for the KLA. And Mr. Limaj also said that at the time of the incident in Ljudevic he was abroad himself taking care -- he was actually in Switzerland taking care of duties that he had been tasked with by the General Staff.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Could we see this next clip, please.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: [Voiceover] Right. As I recall on certain occasions in your interviews and at certain meetings that we had it was described in an anecdotal form by you, the way in which you first started with patrols; the way people did not trust you or them. Can you explain at least one interesting aspect of how you explained the start and -- It's interesting. Sometime around 1996 we were going to go out to carry out an operation. That was our duty. And I was waiting for the now -- the present ministry of public order, Rexhep Selimi, to come. And we had set the time. And there was a barber there, a neighbour of mine there in the village and I was waiting for him to come because that was our meeting place. From the conversation that was going on in the barbershop -- the talk was about the KLA that at that time was still not talked about much -- they started to discuss among themselves: how many Serbs there were, how many men of Seselj and how many of Arkan and who was behind them and what was going on; whether the Serbs were killing each other for various reasons, for certain purposes; and who knows. It was a wide-ranging discussion in this case. In the course of this, somebody asked me a direct question about the question, more because I had stayed a lot in Pristina and maybe I knew more than he did. Then the nature of our operations was known [as interpreted], it very secret and it was very difficult. To say that it was ours, there were times when that didn't work. I found and I found an [inaudible]. I said, Listen, if the Serbs have been inventing us, it is to our good. If it is the Serbs who are in fact doing this, we must support it because they're damaging themselves by doing it. Yes, because they're damaging themselves by doing it. That is very true. On the 26th of November, 1997, was perhaps the first time that an organised KLA was launched. What do you think of the case of Mitrovica? In fact, the condition for all the success of all the KLA, or rather, the military leadership throughout the war, was that it was able at certain moments and at the right time to move from one phase of action to another. At the most suitable moments it moved from one phase to the next. The case of Ljudevic is connected to this. Until then, the KLA had made a deep secret of its operations. But it took a difficult step that it would have been hard for any other organisation to do, moving from what you might call an underground conspiracy and war. This was indeed a step that was as brave as it was dangerous. How do you remember Ljudevic? I wasn't present at Ljudevic because I was abroad at the time. I was in Switzerland at the time on other duties assigned by the General Staff, but ...

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: The next clip begins on page 9 of the transcript.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Can you introduce this clip, please.

utterances.speaker: OLE LEHTINEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Here Mr. Limaj is asked a comment by a person called Gelbard who has called KLA a terrorist group. Mr. Limaj is commenting on this and saying KLA has nothing in common with known terrorist groups such as the ETA or IRA.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: And who is this Mr. Gelbard?

utterances.speaker: OLE LEHTINEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: He is Robert Gelbard who was a United States special envoy to the Balkans during the war.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: [Voiceover] Did Gelbard call you terrorists at first? Yes. How far to what extent did this damage you ... how far did you feel branded by this? In fact, Gelbard's statement was tough and difficult for us at the time. But nevertheless, we started from the fact that Gelbard did not have adequate information about the KLA and did not know what the KLA strategy and policy. So in this way this motivated us to become more visible in our operations faster than to --

utterances.speaker: MR. KHAN
utterances.text: I apologise for the interruption.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: That's fine.

utterances.speaker: MR. KHAN
utterances.text: Your Honours, there seems to be discrepancy which Your Honours perhaps have noticed between the translation which appears on the videocassette and the translation that is going to be exhibited by the Prosecution. It's not clear to me which translation is being relied upon, and perhaps we can have some clarification in relation to that. Should we be seeking to follow the transcript on the video or the transcript on hard copy? Because there is a difference in several places. I'm sorry once again for interrupting.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Your Honour, I've noticed that as well. And I believe what has happened here -- I don't believe there are any substantive differences, but what I think happened was when the video was prepared there was certain modifications or changes made to the transcript. And what I -- it was revised, is the word I'm looking for. What I would propose is that we rely on the changes that appear in the -- on the tape, and we will correct the transcript that we have put into evidence and offer that and serve it, of course, on the Defence. If there are any material differences or problems with the translation, we can take that up at that time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: I'm not sure that I understand what you're proposing. What I have detected is not unusual in translation from one language to another: different phraseology expressing essentially the same sort of subject. Now, just occasionally there is a word or two materially different. But so far I have been noting the different word above the word that is here in the written transcript, so I have both. But generally the main sense seems to be there. I have at this stage no idea what use might be made of these words and whether precise words are going to be material. If they are, we're going to have to get an authorised version so that everybody knows where they stand. But if I'm really without knowledge as to how important the words actually used here will be in the ultimate working out of the evidence in this case. And I certainly wouldn't want to suggest that everything that's here should now be, as it were, put through into an authorised version, just so that there can be a casual reference to it in somebody's closing. So perhaps you might with Mr. Kahn and the other counsel look at the question and see whether what is now happening can by and large be left as it is. All of us are aware that there are variations in the phraseology, essentially, of what's being translated. If that will be satisfactory for the ultimate purposes that each of you foresee, we can leave it at that. But if from your discussions it emerges that a need for an assured translation is felt, then of course we would have to ask that that be arranged, Mr. Whiting.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: That's fine, Your Honour. If that's agreeable to the Defence, I will take it upon myself to produce the two different versions and arrange to discuss it with the Defence, and perhaps if there are no issues we can leave it as it is.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you for raising that, Mr. Kahn. Is that satisfactory for the moment?

utterances.speaker: MR. KHAN
utterances.text: It is, and I am grateful to my learned friend.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: If we could just conclude this clip.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: [Voiceover] To become more visible in our operations, persuade them that we were not what they thought we were and we that were not like certain organisations in Europe and that the KLA was something else and --"

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: The next clip begins at the top of page 11 of the transcript.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Could you introduce this clip for us, please, Mr. Lehtinen.

utterances.speaker: OLE LEHTINEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. This clip -- in this part of the interview Fatmir Limaj describes the different forms of warfare by the KLA. He says that the guerrilla tactics were active all the time and then from time to time they were involved in frontal warfare and he -- as examples he gives the fighting in Lapusnik and the fighting in Rahovec.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Could we see this clip, please.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: [Voiceover] The strategy, the entire strategy of the KLA was adapted to the specify conditions of the terrain in which we were in and also the specifics of our military organisation. Our guerrilla activity was never out of the daily agenda, if I can put it that way; it always existed. But the conduct of a frontal war, we did this when we were forced and in places where it suited us. There were cases in which we were -- we inevitably had to fight a frontal war to defend the civilian population, always to defend the civilian population. Can you mention a definite case, a definite battle? A definite battle was for instance the case of Rahovec, where the KLA carried out an act of self-sacrifice entirely to protect the population. There were also cases, for example, at the Lapusnik pass. There were cases in Drenica. That is, there were many cases in which we were forced to join the line directly in a frontal war purely to protect the civilian population, to ... "

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: The last clip from this documentary starts on the middle of page 13 of the transcript.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Could you introduce this last clip, please.

utterances.speaker: OLE LEHTINEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. This clip describes -- Mr. Limaj describes fighting in Rahovec again and he says that he was there as the commander of the 121st Brigade.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: And when again was the battle at Rahovec?

utterances.speaker: OLE LEHTINEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was from the 17th of July, 1998, up until approximately the 21st of July, 1998.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Could we see this clip, please.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: [Voiceover] People would not have trusted us because of our age. But one thing was important. For instance, in the case of the prime minister, of Prime Minister Thaci. We were together in Rahovec and during the fighting we took turns on duty. We were soldiers on the front line, together with the soldiers, so we presented ourselves as men, as representatives of the General Staff or unit commander. For instance, I was commander of the 121st Brigade. They saw us as being at that level. For instance, they considered Hashim as being a representative of the General Staff or of Drenica. And after all that, all the fighting, those who had been at Rahovec and other lines, when the names of people who were members of the General Staff were published they were shocked and they said, We thought the General Staff was in some bunker somewhere, giving out orders and making plans, and that they gave them to you and that you had the privilege of seeing the General Staff and you were the people who brought these to us on the front line. And if anybody said this to us three months ago, that a member of the General Staff would have been on the front line with us, we would have had a heart attack. It is in the interest that Serbia itself never thought that the members of the General Staff were closer to them than even the soldiers. Our bases were always 200 or 300 or 500 metres from the Serb police.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: We are now going to look at various public source documents. If we could turn to the document at tab 31 which is U0037154 to 7155.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Mr. Lehtinen, just generally in connection with this investigation, have there -- have newspaper articles been collected?

utterances.speaker: OLE LEHTINEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Could you explain for the Court where these articles for the most part have been obtained from.

utterances.speaker: OLE LEHTINEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. These articles have been collected from something called the FBIS which is the Foreign Broadcast Information Service, which is a U.S. governmental operation for translating articles from around the world.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Turning to the first document, can you tell us what this is.

utterances.speaker: OLE LEHTINEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is a document from the FBIS dated 3rd of June, 1998, and it's an interview with Mr. Celiku.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: And it appeared where? What is the source of the interview?

utterances.speaker: OLE LEHTINEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: It appears to be a television network in Tirana, Albanian.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: If you could just read the highlighted portions on the screen, please. And if they could be blown up.

utterances.speaker: OLE LEHTINEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: So it's: "Interview with Mr. Celiku, one of the liberation army of Kosovo UCK, commanders of one area in Drenica from Decani by correspondent Asllan Bajrami on 3 June -- recorded." This is Celiku talking. "The greater part of the Drenice territory and of the Llapushe in general is free and under the control of our forces, that is, under the UCK's control. Our forces have had control of the Pristina-Peja highway for one month now starting with the checkpoint at Komorane and further. "During fighting in Gryke e Llaposhnikut, our army caused considerable damage to the enemy in people and military equipment, killing and wounding dozens of enemies. No one from our army ranks suffered any casualties. The enemy, horrified at the heroism of our fires, started to burn houses and kill the innocent civil population."

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: If we could turn to the next page of that document and if you could read the highlighted portion from the screen, please.

utterances.speaker: OLE LEHTINEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's again Mr. Celiku speaking. "Since the start of war, the Albanian political forces have ignored us completely. Indifferent toward our war, they went so far as to dissociate themselves from the war and are disassociating themselves from the people, too. "It is my duty to repeat here once again the position of the UCK central staff -- there can be no talks about Kosovo without the presence of our representatives. Kosovo is dragging," this is in brackets, "all the Albanian territories that are under the Serb, Macedonian, and Montenegrin rule."

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Could this be given a number, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That will be Prosecution Exhibit P37.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: If you turn to the next document which is a photograph, U0034019.

utterances.speaker: MR. KHAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, if I can ask for the sake of clarification because we don't have the original document whether or not that FIBS report is from 1998 or from 1999.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: It's from 1998.

utterances.speaker: MR. KHAN
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Turning now to the next document, which is a photograph. Mr. Lehtinen, what is this photograph?

utterances.speaker: OLE LEHTINEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is a photograph of a sign -- a sign on the side of the road. It's the road that is seen here is the Pristina-Peja highway. And this sign is alongside this road.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: And is it at Lapusnik?

utterances.speaker: OLE LEHTINEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: And did you take this photograph?

utterances.speaker: OLE LEHTINEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: When?

utterances.speaker: OLE LEHTINEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: This was taken in May of 2003.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: And what does the sign depict?

utterances.speaker: OLE LEHTINEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: The sign shows the UCK/KLA emblem, and it pays attribute to the battle in the gorge of Lapusnik on the 9th of May, 1998.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: If this could be given a number, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That will be Prosecution Exhibit P38.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Now, if we could turn to the third binder of documents, tabs 33 to 47, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Could you pause a moment, please, Mr. Whiting. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Turning to the first document in that binder at tab 33. What is this document?

utterances.speaker: OLE LEHTINEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Again, this is a document from FBIS and it's a newspaper article from the Pristina Bujkutin on the 4th of July, 1998.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Could you read the highlighted portion of the article, please, and if it could be blown up.

utterances.speaker: OLE LEHTINEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: It says: "Drenice e Eperme, 3 July. Drenice e Eperme witnessed a special occasion today when soldiers of the units of the Kosovo Liberation Army [UCK] were sworn in. Members of the population also attended the ceremony. Commander Sokoli ['falcon,' evidently a nom de guerre, but also an Albanian surname] reported on the units, and Commander Celiku ['steel,' also either a nom de guerre, or a surname] reviewed the troops. The participants saluted the national flag and the servicemen were solemnly sworn in. "Commander Celiku said in his speech that our army was born and has grown up in war. It is spreading not by the inch but by the mile. We will continue the struggle we have begun until all the occupied territory of Albania is liberated. The seriousness, morale, and strength of the UCK is becoming apparent every day and the UCK is becoming recognised as an important factor. It has deep roots in the people and is as inseparable from them as flesh is from the bone."

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Could this document be given a number, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That will be Prosecution Exhibit P39.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: If we could turn to the next document at tab 34.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Could you tell us what this is, please.

utterances.speaker: OLE LEHTINEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is a telephone record about fighting still continuing in Lapusnik. And it's dated on the 26th of July, 1998.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Could this be given a number, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That will be Prosecution Exhibit P40.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: The next document at tab 35. What is this?

utterances.speaker: OLE LEHTINEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is another article, and it's headed "Police 'crush terrorist groups' at Lapusnik." It's dated 27th of July, 1998.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: And from the first line of the text, what is the source of this?

utterances.speaker: OLE LEHTINEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: It seems to be the newspaper Tanjug.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Can this be given a number, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That would be Prosecution Exhibit P41.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Next document at tab 36 is a photograph marked U0034003.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Mr. Lehtinen, did you take this photograph?

utterances.speaker: OLE LEHTINEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: And what is depicted in the photograph?

utterances.speaker: OLE LEHTINEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is a memorial of a man called Ali B. Zogaj who has died on the 26th of July, 1998, and this memorial is in Lapusnik at one of the described fighting positions on the slope along the mountain in Lapusnik.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Could this be given a number, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That would be Prosecution Exhibit P42.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: The next document, tab 37.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: What is this, please?

utterances.speaker: OLE LEHTINEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is again an article about Lapusnik headed: "KIC names casualties of Lapusnik, Malisevo, and Pec fighting." It's dated on the 28th of July, 1998.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Could this be given an exhibit number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That will be Prosecution Exhibit P43.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: The next document, please, at tab 38.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: What is this, Mr. Lehtinen?

utterances.speaker: OLE LEHTINEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's a newspaper article from -- dated on the 3rd of September, 1998, headed: "UCK commander of Lapusnik and Kacanik battles."

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: And what is the source?

utterances.speaker: OLE LEHTINEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: The source is called Zeri I Kosoves. And it seems to be published in Zurich, Switzerland.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Who is the interview with?

utterances.speaker: OLE LEHTINEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: This interview is with Commander Celiku.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Turning to the second page of the text, could you please read the highlighted portion of the text and if it could be blown up on the screen.

utterances.speaker: OLE LEHTINEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: So this is a question by the newspaper. "This fire of war burned the enemies in the strait of Lapusnik where you were in command, and it was ^personified in the strait of Kacanik." And this is Commander Celiku: "There was combat and resistance there that only the Albanians know how to carry out. With the assistance of other units that were positioned on the other side of the strait, the Pellumbi and Guri units, and of course with the sacrifice and fighting spirit of our three units, we dealt a strong blow to the enemy who will remember us for a long time because of the losses we inflicted upon him. The maintaining of the strait of Lapusnik for our army and people has had special significance because this strait increased the importance of our army. This strait made it possible to transport the people and to arm them on a massive level and it became the organic linking point for the liberated territories." The newspaper again: "We have learned only about the successes of our army, but have not these successes begun to diminish recently?" Then commander Celiku: "No. There has been no diminishment and there is no reason for defeatism. Simultaneously, there was a withdrawal of forces and a courageous combat. We fought against 138 tanks, surface-to-surface rockets and Katusha rockets, mine launchers of all calibres, and chemical poisons. The soldiers fought against this arsenal of the aggressor. The withdrawal of forces took place only after the people withdrew to secure places and after their defence was assured. We were fighting at a distance of a dozen metres. After the combat ended, we analysed the situation and concluded that we were winners from a military point of view. We had minimal losses, only two of our soldiers were killed, while enemy losses were more than 100. We maintained the military factor which is decisive in a war. "From a strategic aspect we lost control in some places, but we cannot call this a diminishment of our successes, because we are aware that a war is not lost or won on the basis of one battle. We are prepared and we are determined to carry our war to the end and our war will end with the liberation and unification of the Albanian lands which is our military pledge and the political programme of the UCK." And this is the newspaper again: "Since you brought up the political programme, we will ask you a political question: What do you think of Rugova's elections?" And Commander Celiku replies: "You expressed it very well. Rugova's elections. They were Rugova's and no one else's."

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: The battle he is talking about is the battle at the end of July, July 26, 1998?

utterances.speaker: OLE LEHTINEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's what it appears to be.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Could this be given a number, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That will be Prosecution Exhibit P44.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Turning to the next tab, tab 39. What is this?

utterances.speaker: OLE LEHTINEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is an interview with the Pristina Java on the 20th of February 2003. It's an interview with Mr. Fatmir Limaj after the indictment of the ICTY.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Turning to the second page of this interview, could you read the highlighted question and answer, please.

utterances.speaker: OLE LEHTINEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's someone called Desku asking the question. "It is being said that the three others arrested by The Hague were your soldiers. Is this true?" And Mr. Limaj replies: "The truth is that they were in various units. They were in my unit, but also in other units."

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Could this document be given a number, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That will be Prosecution Exhibit P45.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: The next document at tab 40, Mr. Lehtinen, what is this?

utterances.speaker: OLE LEHTINEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is a missing persons report from the OSCE, Kosovo Verifications Mission.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: And how was it observed?

utterances.speaker: OLE LEHTINEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: This has been obtained from the OSCE.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Do you know the date of this report?

utterances.speaker: OLE LEHTINEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I don't know the exact day.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Do you know if it's from after the war?

utterances.speaker: OLE LEHTINEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it's from after the war.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Turning to the second page. I won't ask you to read the text, but it's reporting the missing of which person?

utterances.speaker: OLE LEHTINEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's about the person called Hasan Hoxha.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: And the circumstances they are describing are the circumstances of his disappearance?

utterances.speaker: OLE LEHTINEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Could this be given a number, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That will be Prosecution Exhibit P46.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Tab 41, what is this, please.

utterances.speaker: OLE LEHTINEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is an article in a Serbian newspaper called Dnevnik on the 29th of June, 1998, about three kidnapped Albanians.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: And it's -- who are the three who are kidnapped?

utterances.speaker: OLE LEHTINEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: The three named persons are Agim Ademi, Vesel Ahmeti and Sucri Zumeri.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Do you know anything about this newspaper?

utterances.speaker: OLE LEHTINEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know it's based in Novi Sad.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Could we turn to the next --

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Oh, I'm sorry. The exhibit number, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That will be Prosecution Exhibit P47.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: If we could turn to the collection of documents at tab 42 which is U0038552 through 8690.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Could you tell us, Mr. Lehtinen, what this collection of documents is.

utterances.speaker: OLE LEHTINEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is a group of reports and articles which is -- which are KLA -- Kosovo Liberation Army -- communiques, political, and policy statements.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: From what time period, approximately?

utterances.speaker: OLE LEHTINEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's from before the war and during the war.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Looking at the first one at 8552, could you read the highlighted portion of that first KLA communique.

utterances.speaker: OLE LEHTINEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. "Pristina Kosova daily report number 1144. In English, 20 May 1997. "In a press release communique number 33 faxed to the media, the UCK said it killed Hetem Dobruna at the Llozice village of Klina earlier this month, because of his 'notorious and open collaboration with the Serbian occupying authorities.'"

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Now these were published in various newspapers?

utterances.speaker: OLE LEHTINEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Turning to 8554 which is two pages away, and appears on the screen. Could you read the highlighted portion of that communique, please, number 35, which was published in Pristina Koha Ditore on the 8th of August, 1997.

utterances.speaker: OLE LEHTINEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: "In a communique for the media bearing the number 35. The organisation calling itself 'the Kosovo Liberation Army 'UCK' claims responsibility for recent armed incidents in Kosovo, in which Serbian policemen and two Albanian civilians were injured. This communique states: 'By a decision of the UCK central staff made on 3 and 4 August, our guerrilla units carried out three armed operations against the occupiers and their collaborators.' The organisation also claims responsibility for what are called 'the assassinations of Ali Qullapeku from Terstenik and Ramiz Leku from Baince near Glogovac.' "The communique states: "Because we are dealing with an enemy that understands nothing but the language of force, we are compelled, albeit against our will, to talk down the barrel of a gun; not as a terrorists, but as a liberation organisation that has set itself the task of fighting mercilessly against the invader and his collaborators until the Albanian lands are totally liberated."

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Turn, please, to 8555 from the Pristina Kosova Daily Report, 20 October 1997. Could you read the highlighted portion, please.

utterances.speaker: OLE LEHTINEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. "In similar fax messages bearing neither the date nor the place they were sent from, the alleged UCK has over this and last year claimed responsibility for attacks against members of the Serbian police in Kosovo and Albanians dubbed as 'collaborators of the Serbian regime in Kosovo.'"

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Turn please to 8556, public communique from the Tirana Television Network in Albania, 24 November 1997. Could you please read the highlighted text.

utterances.speaker: OLE LEHTINEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: "The communique stressed that every collaborator who, in this or that form, causes harm to the Albanian national issue is to suffer."

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Turn please to 8557. Communique number 40 of the UCK from -- published in Pristina Bujku, 5 December, 1997. Could you read the highlighted text, please.

utterances.speaker: OLE LEHTINEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: "On the evening of 28 November, Dalip Dugolli, a collaborator and one of Milosevic's most trusted men, was killed in the village of Petreshice near Shtime."

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Turn to 8560 published in Pristina Bujku 1998. Could you read the highlighted portion, please.

utterances.speaker: OLE LEHTINEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: "On 13 February 1990, Mustafe Kurti, a collaborator with the occupier, was liquidated. The communique containing a threat to the Albanian prime minister fabricated by the anti-Albanian circles and released in the name of the UCK is not ours and is invalid."

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Turn now to 8561 communique for Pristina Bujku, 4 March 1998. Could you read the highlighted sentence.

utterances.speaker: OLE LEHTINEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: "Death to enemies and traitors!"

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Turn please to 8573, communique number 47, 13 May 1998, Pristina Koha Ditore. Could you read the highlighted text, please.

utterances.speaker: OLE LEHTINEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: "On the orders of UCK General Staff, successive operations against the invasion troops were carried out in Operational Zone number 1, that is in the operational subzones of Drenica, Erenik, Dukagijn, Pashtrik, and Llap. "Throughout this period, operations were also carried out against Albanian collaborationists, who despite earlier warnings did not abandon their anti-national course of actions."

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Turn to 8575, policy statement number 3 of the KLA published in Pristina Bujku in Albanian, 12 June 1998. Could you read the highlighted phrase, please.

utterances.speaker: OLE LEHTINEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: "The UCK General Staff had decided to appoint Professor Jakup Krasniqi as its spokesman."

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Turn please to 8577, communique number 49, Pristina Koha Ditore in Albanian, 13 July 1998. Could you please read the highlighted section.

utterances.speaker: OLE LEHTINEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: "Measures have also been taken against certain die-hard collaborators, who are still working against our national interests. Operations are underway to reinforce and extend the positions under the control of our forces in the subzones of Pashtrik, Llap, Drenica, Karadak and Dukagijn, within Operational Zone Number 1. Our formations have successfully carried out large-scale operations in the subzone of Pashtrik."

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Turn now to 8580. This is an interview with Mr. Jakup Krasniqi, the spokesman of the KLA published in Pristina Koha Ditore, 11 July 1998. Could you read, please, the highlighted section on this a page.

utterances.speaker: OLE LEHTINEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: "First of all, the Albanian political parties must recognise the UCK as the entirety of the armed forces of Kosovo, and recognise the present situation as a state of war."

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Turning to the next page of that same interview at 8581. Could you read the highlighted section in the first paragraph at the top of the page.

utterances.speaker: OLE LEHTINEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: "The UCK is a liberation army and a regular military formation. It is not an organisation or group that goes in for small-scale actions. Our operations are rather larger, and bear a greater resemblance to those of a regular army."

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: And now the next highlighted portion.

utterances.speaker: OLE LEHTINEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: "The UCK General Staff had its say before the elections in Kosovo, and firmly took the view that the elections should not be held in time of war, because a part of Kosovo was in flames."

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Turning to the next page of this interview with the KLA spokesman, 8582, could you read the highlighted portion there.

utterances.speaker: OLE LEHTINEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is Mr. Krasniqi speaking. "One thing must be made clear. We call him a president even though in many ways he does not deserve the name."

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: And who is he speaking about there?

utterances.speaker: OLE LEHTINEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe he is speaking about Mr. Ibrahim Gugova.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Could you read the next highlighted section, please.

utterances.speaker: OLE LEHTINEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Then Krasniqi: "No. We considered that Ibrahim Rugova has committed a series of political mistakes, to the detriment of national cause, starting from the agreement on education, which came to nothing. "He is the main divisive factor."

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: The next page of the interview, please, at 8583.

utterances.speaker: OLE LEHTINEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: "Rugova is a pacifist and he is often said to believe in Gandhism." He is not a pacifist but a doormat. Rugova will not allow resistance but only subservience, letting yourself be trampled underfoot. We have lost our dignity as individuals, families and a nation. This is true of one-half of the nation. The philosophy of the UCK is to restore to these people their human, family, and national dignity, and to respond the enemy's barbaric violence with a liberation struggle."

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: I'm going to skip the portion at the bottom of the page. If we can turn to the next page. If you can read the highlighted portion at the bottom of the next page. This is 8584.

utterances.speaker: OLE LEHTINEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: "The people of Kosovo are now on a war footing and are in action. We are moving in the direction of creating the institutions of war at the national level, which means that we will not create what you call lists, but national institutions of a war footing." Koha Ditore asks: "What will the UCK do if someone enters into negotiations with Serbia without consulting you?" Krasniqi answers: "We will continue the war."

utterances.speaker: MR. TOPOLSKI
utterances.text: That's okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: If we could turn to 8586, which is the continuation of the interview on the following day. It's published in Pristina Koha Ditore, 12 July, 1998.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: And if you could read the highlighted portions of this continuation of the interview with Mr. Krasniqi.

utterances.speaker: OLE LEHTINEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is Mr. Krasniqi speaking again: "The UCK is a new army in the process of formation. However, the UCK has had its own staff and its military hierarchy from the start, and still has today. "The UCK is an organised army." And Krasniqi continues: "No area of Kosovo has been able to arm itself without the supervision and organisation of the responsible people in the UCK. "It is at a certain level in the hierarchy in which we have apportioned operational zones. These are military secrets, but there is also a hierarchy of the operational zones."

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Could we turn to 8589. And it -- could you read Mr. Krasniqi's response in the middle of the page, please.

utterances.speaker: OLE LEHTINEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: "The international community has criticised the violation of human rights in the kidnapping of Serbian and Montenegrin civilians. What can you say about this?" And Krasniqi answers: "It does indeed seem to us ridiculous to equate the operations of the UCK with those of the Serbian occupier, which are notorious throughout the world. On this point, it seems to me that the international community is not respecting its conventions, starting with the UN charter, et cetera, because the UCK has never dealt with civilians or only if they have been in the service of the army and the police and have done serious hard [sic] to the people and the Albanian national cause. There have been cases in which they have been kidnapped, but in this event they have been handed over to international organisations, of course when they have been innocent. First of all, all Serbian forces, whether the police, the military, or armed civilians, are our enemy. "From the start, we had our own internal rules for our operations. These clearly lay down that the UCK recognises the Geneva Convention and the conventions governing the conduct of war -- even though it has not been offered the chance of signing them, as it would have done. We do not go in for kidnapping. Even if some people have suffered, these have been more Albanian collaborators than Serbian civilians. We do not deal with civilians, and we return those whom we take as prisoners of war. A few days ago we handed over two Serbs originating from Croatia to the International Red Cross. Those we have kidnapped are either announced in a list or reported to be executed, but we do not behave in a base fashion like Serbia -- we do not behave in a base fashion like Serbia." Sorry.
