utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Lehtinen. The reference to "two Serbs originating from Croatia," who that is reference to?

utterances.speaker: OLE LEHTINEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is a reference to witnesses in this case.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Which two witnesses, please?

utterances.speaker: OLE LEHTINEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: These are called Vojko and (redacted).

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Turning please to 8603. This is Pristina Koha Ditore, 12 September, 1998. Could you read the highlighted portion of this statement, please.

utterances.speaker: OLE LEHTINEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: "The UCK and the Albanian people are being stabbed in the back by collaborationist and pacifist elements. "The General Staff of the UCK calls on the Albanian people in general and the people in Kosovo in particular to be vigilant against the misinformation of the enemy and the wicked pacifists, because the UCK did not take up arms simply to surrender them, but to fight for freedom. "Let the chickens cluck for the pitiful pacifists, even while they are alive."

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Turn please to 8606, statement of the General Staff of the KLA, published in Pristina Koha Ditore on 19 September 1998. If you could read the highlighted portion.

utterances.speaker: OLE LEHTINEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: "Punitive measures of various kinds are also being undertaken against collaborationist elements that continue to serve the occupying power."

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Your Honour I would ask that this collection of documents be given a number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That collection will be Prosecution Exhibit P48.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Turning now to the documents at tab 43.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Mr. Lehtinen, what are these documents, please?

utterances.speaker: OLE LEHTINEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: These are copies of the -- of parts of the original newspaper articles that were translated in the earlier batch.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: So to be clear, these are originals of some of the articles that are included in the original batch -- or, the prior batch?

utterances.speaker: OLE LEHTINEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Exactly.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Your Honour, with the assistance of the usher, I actually have a chart which corresponds the documents in this collection to the documents in the prior collection. If they could be distributed, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Not every document that is in this batch at tab 43 has a corresponding English translation in the prior exhibit, though nearly all of them do. And the chart makes it clear which ones correspond. The Prosecution would seek to rely only on those documents that are in Albanian in this collection which have a corresponding translation in the prior exhibit. However, I included all of them simply because it's part of one ERN range. And I would ask now that this collection of documents which is 0081603 to 1636 and the chart that I have just distributed be given a number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: The Albanian articles from ERN number EU0081603 to 1636 will be Prosecution Exhibit P49. And the corresponding English ERN numbers will be 49 -- Prosecution Exhibit P49.1.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: The chart, you mean?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: The chart.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Turning now please to the document that is at tab 44. Mr. Lehtinen, could you tell us what this is, please.

utterances.speaker: OLE LEHTINEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is a judgement in a case that was tried a court in Pristina. It's a war crimes case from -- where the incidents took place in the later part of 1998.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: And when was the trial held? Was it held after the war?

utterances.speaker: OLE LEHTINEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. The trial was held after the war.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: And was it before -- what kind of court? Can you describe the court and the proceedings.

utterances.speaker: OLE LEHTINEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. This case was investigated by international investigators in Kosovo and brought by international prosecutors, and the judges in this case were international.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: And it pertains to what area in Kosovo?

utterances.speaker: OLE LEHTINEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's an area in the north-east of Kosovo. It was called the Llap Operational Zone. And there were KLA detention facilities in the following villages, which are: Bajgora, Lapashtica, Majac, Potok, and Koljic. The first four ones are in the municipality of Podujeva. And Koljic is in the municipality of Pristina, but north of Pristina, close to Podujeva.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: And the time period I think you said pertains to the latter half of -- or late 1998 from August/September 1998?

utterances.speaker: OLE LEHTINEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: August, September, October of 1998, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: If you could just -- and the date of the judgement is 16 July, 2003?

utterances.speaker: OLE LEHTINEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: If you could just read the highlighted portion on the first page which will continue on to the second page.

utterances.speaker: OLE LEHTINEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: "In relation to Latif Gashi, aka commander Lata. "During the period 30th October 1998 to late April 1999 in complicity with Rrustem Mustafa, and aided and abetted by Nazif Mehmeti and others and pursuant to a joint criminal plan, he illegally detained Kosovo Albanian citizens suspected of collaboration with Serbs in a detention centre organised by and under the control of the KLA at Lapashtica and also at Majac and Potok, by causing them to be detained in an inhumane conditions, depriving them of adequate sanitation and beating and torturing them, thus causing them great suffering and violation of their health and thereby depriving them of their right to a fair trial. "The purpose of the plan being to seek to force those detailed to confess to disloyalty to the KLA and to punish those detailed for that alleged disloyalty to the KLA, Count 2, 5, and 8. Sorry, I'll start from the beginning. "During the period 31st May, 1999, until an unknown date in mid-June 1999, at an unknown location in Koliq in complicity with Naim Kadriu he illegally detained beat and tortured Witnesses Q and R, thus exposing them to great suffering and violation of bodily health, and thereby depriving them of their right to a fair trial (Count 3 and 9). "During the period 1st August 1998, to 26 September 1998, at a detention centre organised by and under the control of KLA at Bajgora, he beat and tortured Milovan Stankovic, thereby exposing him to great suffering and violation of bodily health and thus aided and abetted the unlawful detention of Milovan Stankovic. (Count 12 and 14.)"

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Could you turn please to page 1484 by ERN number and 21 by judgement number of this judgement and now read the highlighted portion.

utterances.speaker: OLE LEHTINEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: "In the vast majority of cases, persons were detained for reasons that the trial panel found were insufficient, sometimes grossly so, even for the preliminary step of arrest to be justified. In those cases, detention was arbitrary from the moment of arrest. In cases where the trial panel found that the reasons could justify arrest, it was clear that no independent process of review, nor any subsequent judicial process was established by which a detainee could challenge the order for his or her detention. In all cases, the intention to prosecute detainees for their alleged offenses or other violations according to the KLA was pursued in breach of the requirements of Common Article 3 and Protocol II. "The evidence in the case indicates that whether or not a detainee was released from detention depended on the view of the senior KLA commanders and no one else. In this case, the trial panel found that during the armed conflict of 1998 and 1999 Kosovar Albanians accused of being collaborators were forcibly abducted, or in some cases summoned and placed into detention for alleged infractions that were at best ill-defined. The essence of the allegations varied, although in most cases the effect was to assert that the conduct of such persons was inappropriate or disloyal to the KLA. It was clear from the evidence of the defendants that the detention of the detainees was effected with a view to some form of summary trial process being carried out. The fact that such trial proceedings as took place lacked basic judicial guarantees, and yet the detention of many persons was maintained leads inevitably to the conclusion that the detention of those persons was a blatant breach of Article 9 of the ICCPR, Common Article 3 and Article 6 of Protocol III. The absence of any clear legal directives by the KLA governing detention and trial in areas of Kosovo under KLA control only serves to aggravate this situation."

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Now turning to page 84 of the judgement, which is 1547 by ERN number. In the interests of saving time, expediting, I would just ask you to read the last paragraph on that page.

utterances.speaker: OLE LEHTINEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: "The trial panel has no doubt that the treatment of detainees at Llapashtica was appalling. As emphasised above, the conditions in the room in which as many as fifteen or sixteen detainees were incarcerated were unquestionably inhuman. Again, as at Bare/Bajgora, the proposition of the defendants that questioning did not take place is simply untrue. "Further, the trial panel finds that those who were detained for substantial periods of time were subject to routine beatings in an attempt to cause them to confess to acts of disloyalty to the KLA, and/or to extract information or confessions from them. The treatment of those detainees thus amounted to torture."

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Your Honour, could this document be given a number, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That will be Prosecution Exhibit P50.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Turning now to tab 45 [sic]. Mr. Lehtinen, what is at that tab?

utterances.speaker: OLE LEHTINEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is a decision and a correction to the previous judgement where a date has been wrongly inputted. The correct date at this place is 27th of March, 1999, whereas it has been mentioned as 27th of April, 1999.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Could this be given a number, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That will be Prosecution Exhibit P51.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Turning now to the next document, which is entitled Kosovo Biographical Reporting, Fatmir Limaj.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: What is this document, Mr. Lehtinen?

utterances.speaker: OLE LEHTINEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, this is a biographical reporting on Mr. Fatmir Limaj by the U.S. office in Pristina.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: What is the date of the document?

utterances.speaker: OLE LEHTINEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's dated on the 2nd of March, 2001.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: And how was it obtained?

utterances.speaker: OLE LEHTINEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: This has been received from the United States government.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Turning please to the second page of the document at number 5. Could you please read the highlighted portion.

utterances.speaker: OLE LEHTINEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: "With the outbreak of war in Kosovo in spring 1998, Limaj became one of the first KLA commanders to go public - using his nickname 'Celiku' (steel). Initially Limaj served for five months as a brigade commander in the Malisevo area, where he gained the reputation of being harsh and stubborn. Observers from the Kosovo diplomatic observer mission, KDOM, and the OSCE Kosovo Verification Mission, KVM, found him very hard to negotiate with, and were unable to persuade him to restrain his soldiers from shooting at police patrols. That fall, Limaj became a member of the KLA General Staff."

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Could this be given a number, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That could be Prosecution Exhibit P52.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: The next document, please, K0310973 to 0979.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: What is this document?

utterances.speaker: OLE LEHTINEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is a statement by the Serb police. It's a statement from a person called Hisni Murseli.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: What is the date of the statement?

utterances.speaker: OLE LEHTINEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's the 10th of January, 1999.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: How was this statement obtained?

utterances.speaker: OLE LEHTINEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: This -- we have received this as part of a large number of documents that were seized from the Pristina court in June of 1999, immediately after the war.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: They were seized under what authority?

utterances.speaker: OLE LEHTINEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: They were seized under warrant from the tribunal.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: From the Pristina court?

utterances.speaker: OLE LEHTINEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Has this document then been in the custody of the tribunal since that time, approximately June of 1999?

utterances.speaker: OLE LEHTINEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Now, do you know -- have you learned if Mr. Murseli, the person whose statement it is, is still alive?

utterances.speaker: OLE LEHTINEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I've learned that this person called Hisni Murseli is not alive.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: How did you learn that?

utterances.speaker: OLE LEHTINEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I've spoken to his brother and I've learned that he was -- he died in January of 1999.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: What did he tell you about what he knew first of all about his detention and then subsequently about his death?

utterances.speaker: OLE LEHTINEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Murseli's brother told me that around the 8th of January, 1999, his brother was arrested by the Serb police and that is the last he knows about him. Approximately 20 days later, the family of Hisni Murseli is informed that Mr. Murseli had died and the body could be recovered from the morgue in Pristina.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Lehtinen, do you know from this document what the -- whether the information that was provided by Mr. Murseli was -- or purports to be provided by Mr. Murseli was in fact provided by him or was simply put down on the paper by those interviewing him?

utterances.speaker: OLE LEHTINEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is impossible to say.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Could you read the highlighted portion, please, of the first page of the interview.

utterances.speaker: OLE LEHTINEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: "In May 1998, I arrived to the country from Slovenia, where I was temporarily working. I came so as to actively join the KLA, which I did shortly after in my village Nekovac. Territorially, my village came under the KLA Celiku unit, which was led my Fatmir Limaj, from Banja village, near Malisevo."

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Turning now to page 4 of the interview. Could you read the highlighted portion, please.

utterances.speaker: OLE LEHTINEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: "I know that KLA units were also organised in other villages, such as Sedlare, where the staff was in the 'Karpuzi' town quarter; in the Sopi and Gasi town quarters in Lapusnik, which numbered about 70 members; one in Donja Fustica, with 10 members; and one in Gornja Fustica, with 26 members. There were no other organised units in Komorane, except for those in the Viljak and Buzalja town quarters, which were near Kisna Reka. All these units fell under the Celiku KLA military formation commanded with Fatmir Limaj, which had staffs in Klecka and Berisa villages."

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Turning now to the next page, please. Could you read the highlighted portion.

utterances.speaker: OLE LEHTINEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: "During the combat action between the MUP and the KLA in Lapusnik - where the KLA controlled a part of the Pristina-Pec main road - a large number of KLA members were deployed at positions in Lapusnik. During the first days, my unit was not sent to these positions since Fatmir Limaj thought there were enough forces already present. However, following the withdrawal of the Plumbi KLA forces from that area to the Pogrk town quarter of Lapusnik, Fatmir Limaj personally came to Kisna Reka and ordered us to the positions in Lapusnik. Around 0200 hours that same night, my department went on foot to Lapusnik, where we took up positions in the trenches in the 'Sopi' town quarter. In the morning, we fought with the MUP members, and then after a few hours of armed combat, retreated towards Berisa village. "Pursuant to orders from Fatmir Limaj, my department was transferred from Berisa village to Negrovac village in order to take part in further combat against MUP members. We were then transferred to the Djurdjica town quarter in Orlate village, Glogovac municipality, where we took up positions and fought with the MUP members. After three or four hours of combat we retreated to Berisa village. I would like to mention that several KLA commander, such as Fatmir Limaj, Shaban Shala, Jakup Krasniqi were staying in Berisa village at that time."

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: If we could turn to page 7 of this report. If you could read this highlighted portion, please.

utterances.speaker: OLE LEHTINEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: "I would like to add that there was an improvised prison in the Gashi town quarter in Lapusnik, where KLA members detained kidnapped Serbs and Albanians. I know that the prison was a type of bunker, dug out under the ground and located at Shaqir Vojvoda's house in the vicinity of Bali Vojvoda's house where one of the KLA staffs is headquartered. There were about 35 Serbs detained in this prison and about as many Albanians. As far as I know, just before the clash between the MUP and the KLA in Lapusnik, the detainees from this prison were transferred to Klecka and I don't know what happened to them subsequently. "The Albanians that were detained in the prison were labelled as being 'Serbian spies.' I know that Hazir Dugolli from Nekovac, and Shaban Syliqi, from Kisna Reka were amongst the detainees. As far as Shaban Syliqi is concerned, I know that he spent two or three months in the prison at the beginning of summer 1998 - between May and June approximately - and was freed by Commander Maliq Vilaku, who vouched that he was not a 'spy' and that he had complete trust in him. Immediately upon his release, Shaban Syliqi joined the KLA and received a 20 rifle from Maliq and was later issued with a Gulinov-type heavy machine-gun."

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Could this be given a number, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That will be Prosecution Exhibit P53.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: That may be a convenient time, Mr. Whiting.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: We will resume at 10 minutes to.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Whiting.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. We've now completed with the third binder, and there's just one remaining exhibit which is the Victims booklet, collection of photographs, which I hope has been provided.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Mr. Lehtinen, do you have the book of victims in front of you?

utterances.speaker: OLE LEHTINEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: It is labelled "Killed Victims and Surviving Victims." Can you tell us what is contained in this booklet.

utterances.speaker: OLE LEHTINEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: These are pictures of victims related to the case and there is two sections; the first section is killed victims and the later section is surviving victims. And each picture has the ERN number of a photograph and the name of the person. And at the beginning --

utterances.speaker: MR. KHAN
utterances.text: Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KHAN
utterances.text: I just rise to note the obvious. It does appear there is a problem with the LiveNote. It's not up to speed, as it were.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mine is.

utterances.speaker: MR. KHAN
utterances.text: Ours is not, Your Honour. I think my friend can continue as long as it's on the -- the transcript is available. Hopefully it can be solved from outside the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you. Technical help is on its way.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: If you can proceed, if you remember where you were in your answer.

utterances.speaker: OLE LEHTINEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. At the beginning of both the sections there is an index with the names and the ERN numbers and it also indicates the page number or consecutive number of the photographs in each section.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Can you tell us how these photographs were obtained.

utterances.speaker: OLE LEHTINEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: The photographs of killed victims have been gathered from families and relatives of the victims. And for the survived victims, they have been obtained from the persons themselves in question.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: And from those sources, have you been able to confirm that each person who is identified in the photograph is actually that person?

utterances.speaker: OLE LEHTINEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm not going to go through these photographs, but I ask that this booklet be given a number, please, and it also be under seal.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Your Honour, can I have one more comment on this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Yes. If you have another comment.

utterances.speaker: OLE LEHTINEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I wanted to comment on the list of killed victims. They all have -- they are all of some relation to the investigation with the exception -- and each of them will be described as witnesses to have some relation to the prison camp in Lapusnik, except for number 25 of the killed victims, who is related to the disappearance and his -- to the disappearance of other prisoners. And he -- and the disappearance of this person happens at the same time period. But no witness will mention him in the Lapusnik prison camp.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Lehtinen, for that clarification.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: If this could be given a number, and it be under seal, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That will be Prosecution Exhibit P54, under seal.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Your Honour, I have no further questions of this witness. I just have two procedural matters to attend to. The first is that the witness has marked four maps, maps 5 and 6 and images 7 and 8. I would ask that those be given numbers, and I know that three numbers were reserved already.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Mr. Whiting, the map number 6 from Prosecution Exhibit P1 will be Prosecution Exhibit P2. Image number 7 arising from Prosecution Exhibit P1 will be Prosecution Exhibit P3. Image number 8 arising in Prosecution Exhibit P1 will be Prosecution Exhibit P4. And map number 5 arising from Prosecution Exhibit P1 that was marked today will be Prosecution Exhibit P55 [sic].

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: And these are marked versions of these maps.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Thank you. The second procedural matter is I -- and forgive me if this is unnecessary -- but I would now move all the exhibits into evidence. Perhaps that has already been done. Perhaps it's already been admitted into evidence. I'm just not familiar with the procedural mechanism of this courtroom.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated] when an exhibit is allocated an exhibit number -- I beg your pardon. If it is allocated an exhibit number, the exhibit is in evidence. If it is marked for identification, it is not in evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: And so all these exhibits are into evidence?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOPOLSKI
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOPOLSKI
utterances.text: May I observe that it's a career first that I rise to cross-examine the witness at 6.00 on a Friday evening.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOPOLSKI
utterances.text: Mr. Lehtinen, I think as you already know, I together with Mr. Powles represent Isak Musliu. There are a number of questions I would like to ask you and I would indicate to help you and to help everybody else follow, as it were, headings of areas I would like to ask you about. Can I ask you first of all some questions about your approach to the investigation generally. You have, do you not, considerable experience in Kosovo?

utterances.speaker: OLE LEHTINEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOPOLSKI
utterances.text: Do you in fact speak Albanian?

utterances.speaker: OLE LEHTINEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I don't.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOPOLSKI
utterances.text: You told us yesterday that you served as a police officer there in 2000 and 2001.

utterances.speaker: OLE LEHTINEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOPOLSKI
utterances.text: You were in the region, as you described it, as a peacekeeper in 1995 and 1996. Was that in Kosovo?

utterances.speaker: OLE LEHTINEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: That was not in Kosovo.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOPOLSKI
utterances.text: Not in Kosovo. You have been, have you not, intimately involved in this particular investigation for quite some time?

utterances.speaker: OLE LEHTINEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOPOLSKI
utterances.text: And as I think the most senior investigator we're going to hear from, the person with perhaps the greatest knowledge of it; would that be right?

utterances.speaker: OLE LEHTINEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is right.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOPOLSKI
utterances.text: May I ask you then about how you approached that task, Mr. Lehtinen. As far as you are concerned and for those who you are responsible, would you regard your task as an objective search for the truth?

utterances.speaker: OLE LEHTINEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I would.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOPOLSKI
utterances.text: Or seeking to prove a pre-conceived position? Which?

utterances.speaker: OLE LEHTINEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would chose the first one, to seek for the truth.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOPOLSKI
utterances.text: When conducting interviews, and we'll look later at parts of interviews, would you agree that it's appropriate to avoid asking witnesses leading questions?

utterances.speaker: OLE LEHTINEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I agree.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOPOLSKI
utterances.text: We come from different parts of the same continent of Europe, you and I, so we ought to make sure we understand each other. What do you understand by the meaning of the term "leading question"?

utterances.speaker: OLE LEHTINEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would understand that as being -- asking a question where -- in a way that you actually show what answer you're expecting to get from who you interview.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOPOLSKI
utterances.text: I couldn't have put it better myself, Mr. Lehtinen. I wonder if you could be good enough to look at a file that we have prepared.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOPOLSKI
utterances.text: Your Honours ought to have this. It's entitled "Documents for use in the cross-examination of Mr. Lehtinen." Your Honours should have one each. Your Honours, could I indicate, please, that this bundle was handed to the Prosecution last night for them to consider it overnight.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOPOLSKI
utterances.text: Mr. Lehtinen, what this bundle is is an extract from various documents in the case, you'll appreciate. And I just want to ask you on the subject that we've just been discussing, leading questions, one or two matters, if I may. First of all, the first document is in fact parts of the interview of the witness Shukri Buja. Do you see a tab marked tab 1, Mr. Lehtinen?

utterances.speaker: OLE LEHTINEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOPOLSKI
utterances.text: Could you go to that tab, which ought to be on page 8639. I'm just referring to the last four digits. Do you have that?

utterances.speaker: OLE LEHTINEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I have that.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOPOLSKI
utterances.text: And you are, are you not, the OL referred to on that page?

utterances.speaker: OLE LEHTINEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOPOLSKI
utterances.text: And you can see there that the subject matter of the questioning is at this stage abductions.

utterances.speaker: OLE LEHTINEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOPOLSKI
utterances.text: Could you go. If you want to do it on the internal paging, this is page 1. If you turn on to page 20 or 8658, whichever you prefer. I want to draw your attention if I may, to a question you ask this witness, who we are going to hear from, just over halfway down. "The times you visited the camp, let's call it a camp, or the main -- this place in Lapusnik." Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: OLE LEHTINEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mm-hmm.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOPOLSKI
utterances.text: And if you go three -- four pages on to internal page 24 or top right-hand corner page 8662, let's just look at how else it is described. By you near the top of the page: "When you went into this place, did you run into guards? So let's call it a prison." Just over halfway down, the witness refers to it as a "point." You refer to it as "the place." Maybe you think this is a silly point, Mr. Lehtinen, I don't know; maybe others do, too. But are you putting words in the witness's mouth there using the word "place"?

utterances.speaker: OLE LEHTINEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, it certainly hasn't been my intention to do so. And am I allowed to -- do you want me to --

utterances.speaker: MR. TOPOLSKI
utterances.text: I've asked you the question. You must answer it.

utterances.speaker: OLE LEHTINEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: These kind of interviews are -- we're going on for a long time, we're talking about this place or what we call it. The witness in this case has certainly not used the word "prison" about it. And there's clearly -- it's, clearly, not clear to us what common name we use for the place in question.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOPOLSKI
utterances.text: Was it your view of this investigation, once you became involved in it, Mr. Lehtinen, that this was a prison, this place? Was that your view of it?

utterances.speaker: OLE LEHTINEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: From reviewing the material that was available when I started the investigation, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOPOLSKI
utterances.text: Let's just have a look at how your general attitude to the issue of prisons may have revealed itself. At the very beginning of this section of this file -- again, as I've indicated one is looking here at parts of the interviews of Shukri Buja. Could I ask you, please, to go to page 18, 8633.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOPOLSKI
utterances.text: Yes. Which on this particular page is just a little way down from the top of it. Do you have that? Internal page 18, 8633. Have you got that?

utterances.speaker: OLE LEHTINEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOPOLSKI
utterances.text: And it's you speaking at the bottom of the page: "You were fighting a war against the Serbs and for the freedom of your people and your country, but the fact is things happened in the area that were not justifiable, even if there was a war going on." That's you speaking, Mr. Lehtinen, is it not?

utterances.speaker: OLE LEHTINEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOPOLSKI
utterances.text: And does it in effect indicate your general approach to the question of camps, that is to say there is nothing necessarily wrong with a camp, it's just a matter of what goes on in it that may be the problem. Do I fairly summarise what seems to be your position in these two statements of yours?

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm going to object to this question. I'm not -- I don't see the relevance of it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: I'd have thought the relevance is self-evident, if I might be a little blunt at this hour. The question is directed to whether words or thoughts were being suggested to the witness rather than the witness's view elicited. The way it was last put was perhaps a little obscure, but --

utterances.speaker: MR. TOPOLSKI
utterances.text: But that's certainly the hour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: So there's a praise each way, Mr. Topolski.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOPOLSKI
utterances.text: Well, thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOPOLSKI
utterances.text: Your approach, your position as senior investigator, the notion of the existence of a camp is of itself not offensive. Do you agree?

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Your Honour, this -- I'm sorry to rise again and object, but this is not asking about how -- about leading questions or about how things are put into witness's minds. This is about his personal opinions about things, and I don't see how that's relevant.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: I have -- we will allow the questioning to continue, Mr. Whiting. I think the drift is clear, that the personal opinion has found itself way into the way propositions were put to the witness. Whether that will be borne out by the answers is another matter.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOPOLSKI
utterances.text: That's all I'm exploring. I'm not going to go on about this.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOPOLSKI
utterances.text: You understand the question, Mr. Lehtinen?

utterances.speaker: OLE LEHTINEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOPOLSKI
utterances.text: What's the answer?

utterances.speaker: OLE LEHTINEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I hope this is not a language problem. I hope I understand camp in the same way. English is not my mother tongue. My answer to your question would be -- my knowledge of it is there is nothing wrong with a camp.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOPOLSKI
utterances.text: This was a war, yes?

utterances.speaker: OLE LEHTINEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOPOLSKI
utterances.text: In war, armies, either official or otherwise, take prisoners, don't they?

utterances.speaker: OLE LEHTINEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOPOLSKI
utterances.text: They interrogate people, don't they?

utterances.speaker: OLE LEHTINEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's also correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOPOLSKI
utterances.text: It is how they are treated that is the subject matter of this trial, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: OLE LEHTINEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Exactly.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOPOLSKI
utterances.text: Let's move away from that to another topic, please, and that is statement-taking itself, in a more general sense. You participated, did you not, personally in the taking of a number of statements in this case and conducting interviews?

utterances.speaker: OLE LEHTINEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOPOLSKI
utterances.text: We'll see a list of those at tab 2 in the file. This may not be exhaustive, but it's certainly indicative, I suggest, 29 interviews and statements you may have never counted, Mr. Lehtinen, all of which involved you as the key participant. Do you agree?

utterances.speaker: OLE LEHTINEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I agree.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOPOLSKI
utterances.text: If you move on to tab 3, you'll see a document the like of which we will see many times in the trial. It's called a witness statement and --

utterances.speaker: MR. TOPOLSKI
utterances.text: Your Honour, before I mention the name of the witness to whom this relates, may I respectfully invite Your Honour to remind me the position as far as naming this individual is concerned. Your Honour sees the surname and the name at tab 3. I don't want to gratuitously mention names if it's not going to be appropriate.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Until this is finally resolved, perhaps as all of us can see the name you cannot expressly identify --

utterances.speaker: MR. TOPOLSKI
utterances.text: L27 is the other way this witness can be described. I'm glad I raised it. I didn't want to give offence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: It was left still a little in the air this afternoon. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOPOLSKI
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOPOLSKI
utterances.text: Let's call him L27, shall we, Mr. Lehtinen?

utterances.speaker: OLE LEHTINEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOPOLSKI
utterances.text: We all know who we're talking about. Were you present when this was prepared?

utterances.speaker: OLE LEHTINEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I was not.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOPOLSKI
utterances.text: No. Have you read it before?

utterances.speaker: OLE LEHTINEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I have read it.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOPOLSKI
utterances.text: Can you go, please, to the second page of it, to the bottom. Again, I just want to understand how these things come to be taken, and it's for the Court to decide in due course what weight they give, of course, to these statements. "The witness wants to change something in the statement," it says at the bottom. Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: OLE LEHTINEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mm-hmm. Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOPOLSKI
utterances.text: "The following," by which I take it to mean this is what the witness now wants to say. "His father was taken after Commandant Qiriqi Ramiz. (He now lives in Lipjan.) He is from a village named Krajmirovc. Qeriqizi [sic] sent and ordered to Qiriqi to arrest his father." Now assume for the purpose of the question that Qerqiz is a reference to my client Isak Musliu. Yes. Assume that for the moment. This seems to be saying that the witness now wants to say that Qerqiz, Musliu, sent an order to Qiriqi, who is a witness for the Prosecution in this case, to make an arrest. That's what's being said here, isn't it? I wonder if you could look at the first part of this witness statement on the previous page and read to yourself, perhaps, just the first dozen or so lines. From the words "two years ago," down to "KPS in Ferzaj." Have you read that, Mr. Lehtinen?

utterances.speaker: OLE LEHTINEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOPOLSKI
utterances.text: If that passage on the second page is intended to change something, considering that the rest of the statement appears to have nothing to do with the original taking of the witness's father, it's that part that the witness seems to want to change, isn't it, by adding this reference to Qerqiz and Qiriqi. Do you agree?

utterances.speaker: OLE LEHTINEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Could I please have that again?

utterances.speaker: MR. TOPOLSKI
utterances.text: Those first few lines are about an abduction. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: OLE LEHTINEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOPOLSKI
utterances.text: That's about being taken to Lapusnik and put in an outhouse and they are about being -- the arrest and why somebody was being arrested. Correct?

utterances.speaker: OLE LEHTINEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOPOLSKI
utterances.text: Okay, by the commander of the jail. And then a person named Musliu visits every three or four days. He was the commander of one area, fighting area. So what this witness is now wanting to change is he wants to say something more about Qerqiz and ordering an arrest. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: OLE LEHTINEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOPOLSKI
utterances.text: You've conducted a number of interviews yourself, as we've seen. When witnesses are interviewed and things are written down, how does it work, Mr. Lehtinen? Is everything written and then read over to the witness?

utterances.speaker: OLE LEHTINEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's how it happens.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOPOLSKI
utterances.text: And each witness is given the opportunity of adding, altering, or changing anything he or she wishes; is that right?

utterances.speaker: OLE LEHTINEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOPOLSKI
utterances.text: Have you ever, for example - and I don't suggest there's anything wrong in doing so - said to a witness at the end of this sort of process said, Can you help us any more about a particular topic?

utterances.speaker: OLE LEHTINEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I guess I would have asked if there's any more information to provide, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOPOLSKI
utterances.text: Yes. If, for example, you get the feeling as an experienced police officer that the witness may have more to say, that would be a reason for doing so.

utterances.speaker: OLE LEHTINEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOPOLSKI
utterances.text: I suppose another reason would be if you think the witness hasn't said enough. You agree?

utterances.speaker: OLE LEHTINEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I agree.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOPOLSKI
utterances.text: Well, I can't ask you anymore about this because you weren't there, but I just wanted to take that as an example. Let me move on to another aspect of the statement taking and investigation process. At tab 4 we see a photo line-up. We're going to see this many times, I imagine, in this trial. This is one that features at number 2 the client I represent. Mr. Lehtinen, were you involved in the choice of photographs that went to the making of this line-up?

utterances.speaker: OLE LEHTINEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I was.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOPOLSKI
utterances.text: Were you throughout this investigation satisfied as to the procedures that were followed when photographs such as these were shown to witnesses?

utterances.speaker: OLE LEHTINEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far -- to my knowledge, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOPOLSKI
utterances.text: Are you aware of any circumstance or circumstances where that procedure was not followed, the proper procedure I mean?

utterances.speaker: OLE LEHTINEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Are we now talking about this line-up?

utterances.speaker: MR. TOPOLSKI
utterances.text: This line-up and line-ups generally.

utterances.speaker: OLE LEHTINEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Concerning the ones done by the investigators in the ICTY, I have not -- no information.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOPOLSKI
utterances.text: All right. As you were the one who assisted or perhaps created this line-up, may I ask you this: Upon what basis was this particular photograph of Musliu chosen?

utterances.speaker: OLE LEHTINEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: The photograph of Mr. Musliu, to my recollection, it was the only photograph we had.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOPOLSKI
utterances.text: The only photograph you had. But we have others of him, don't we? Three, don't we? You've got your bundle there, exhibits tabs 1 to 20. We looked at these yesterday. Would you please go to tab 9. Would you please, with your finger in tab 9, turn to tab 10. 9 was recovered from Musliu's house, wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: OLE LEHTINEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOPOLSKI
utterances.text: And so was 10.

utterances.speaker: OLE LEHTINEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOPOLSKI
utterances.text: Yes. Is it the position that you're telling us, Mr. Lehtinen, that you did not have those two photographs of Musliu, tabs 9 and 10, at a time when you were interviewing witnesses. Is that the position?

utterances.speaker: OLE LEHTINEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is correct, to a part.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOPOLSKI
utterances.text: To a part.

utterances.speaker: OLE LEHTINEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Until the searches were done.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOPOLSKI
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: OLE LEHTINEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOPOLSKI
utterances.text: Would you agree that his appearance in tab 9 is rather different from his appearance at line-up photograph number 2?

utterances.speaker: OLE LEHTINEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is very much correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOPOLSKI
utterances.text: Yes. Did you ever go back to a single witness to whom you'd shown line-up photo 2 with a copy of photograph behind tab 9?

utterances.speaker: OLE LEHTINEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: There has been a line-up done with the new photograph, but I -- now I cannot remember. I would have to check my material if it's been shown to someone who has been shown the picture earlier.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOPOLSKI
utterances.text: Well, it may be that you're going to have to research that for us, Mr. Lehtinen. Would you be good enough to do so? The question I've asked you is whether any witness was shown a photograph of Musliu -- showing him in the way he's shown in photograph 9. You understand the question?

utterances.speaker: OLE LEHTINEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: If that is the question, the answer is yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOPOLSKI
utterances.text: The answer is question.

utterances.speaker: OLE LEHTINEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: If the question is whether a witness has been shown a picture of him from the tab 9.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOPOLSKI
utterances.text: The answer is yes?

utterances.speaker: OLE LEHTINEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOPOLSKI
utterances.text: Which witness?

utterances.speaker: OLE LEHTINEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I hope it's okay to mention the name.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOPOLSKI
utterances.text: I don't know what you're about to say.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: I don't know the answer to that. I don't know which witness it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOPOLSKI
utterances.text: Well, Mr. Lehtinen, are you aware of if identity of all the protected witnesses in this case?

utterances.speaker: OLE LEHTINEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOPOLSKI
utterances.text: Your Honour, I don't know if it might be appropriate for him to write it down.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: I was just going to suggest it. Thank you, Mr. Topolski. Could the witness be given a pen and paper. Can that be shown to the -- to Mr. Whiting, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Your Honour, it's my belief and Mr. Black's belief as well that we have asked for protective measures for this witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Perhaps the name could be shown to Mr. Topolski.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOPOLSKI
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: And other counsel.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOPOLSKI
utterances.text: Well, without checking it, Your Honour, I work upon the basis that Mr. Whiting is right, and therefore I err on the side of caution and will not mention that witness's name.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOPOLSKI
utterances.text: Mr. Lehtinen, are we therefore to understand that that gentleman, to your recollection, is the only witness to whom a photograph of a bearded Musliu has been shown or are there others?

utterances.speaker: OLE LEHTINEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: To my recollection I think it's the only one.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOPOLSKI
utterances.text: The only one?

utterances.speaker: OLE LEHTINEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOPOLSKI
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Mr. Lehtinen, are you aware that we in fact also have a movie image of Musliu for the relevant time that we're dealing with on video?

utterances.speaker: OLE LEHTINEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot recall that now.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOPOLSKI
utterances.text: No? Well, let me show you. I wonder if we could have on the screen the very opening shots of Prosecution Exhibit P35, the video Mr. Whiting showed us this afternoon, I think.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: I assume, Mr. Topolski, you're asking us to --

utterances.speaker: MR. TOPOLSKI
utterances.text: Oh, I'm sorry. Is that the way it works? I'm sorry. I rather misunderstood something.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Okay. It will just -- Mr. Younis tells me it will take a moment to turn on the Sanction and find the image.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOPOLSKI
utterances.text: I sprung it on him. We can move on. Would it help if we move on?

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: You can do that and we'll let you know as soon as we have it up.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: At this hour, a little self-help doesn't hurt, Mr. Topolski.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOPOLSKI
utterances.text: Sorry. I didn't appreciate the system. I shall never spring that on anyone again. I apologise.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOPOLSKI
utterances.text: On the question of showing the photographs, I used the word "line-up," and I'm asked quite rightly to clarify this. When you say -- when I talk about a photograph of the bearded Musliu being shown to that gentleman, it is a photograph of Mr. Musliu and no one else. Is that right.

utterances.speaker: OLE LEHTINEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's not correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOPOLSKI
utterances.text: Not correct?

utterances.speaker: OLE LEHTINEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's a similar line-up with pictures, again chosen to be similar with the photograph of the beard.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOPOLSKI
utterances.text: Well, I wonder, Mr. Lehtinen, if at some stage you would be good enough to put your hand on that line-up, because I haven't seen it.

utterances.speaker: OLE LEHTINEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I will.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOPOLSKI
utterances.text: Thank you. Let's move away from that subject, coming back to the video where it appears Mr. Younis is ready, to some other questions regarding one or two specific individuals, if I may please, Mr. Lehtinen. The first is this. At T5 in the bundle, there's a statement of a gentleman we're going to hear from relatively shortly I imagine, (redacted). Correct?

utterances.speaker: OLE LEHTINEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOPOLSKI
utterances.text: And T5 ought to be at page 9 of his statement, our page 32184. Is it?

utterances.speaker: OLE LEHTINEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOPOLSKI
utterances.text: Good. Just over halfway down the page begins a paragraph: "During my time in the camp." "During my time in the camp, I didn't see any other prisoners than the ones I mentioned earlier in this statement. About the buildings I can say that the owners of the farm lived in the building marked number 1 on the picture. They were a couple in their late 50s or early 60s. I assumed they were the owners because the woman used to feed the chicken in the yard and the man was sometimes helping with water and such." That's what the paragraph says, is that right?

utterances.speaker: OLE LEHTINEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOPOLSKI
utterances.text: Do you have statements from the farm owners?

utterances.speaker: OLE LEHTINEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOPOLSKI
utterances.text: Do those statements confirm that they were indeed present during these events on the farm?

utterances.speaker: OLE LEHTINEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOPOLSKI
utterances.text: Do those statements in fact show the opposite?

utterances.speaker: OLE LEHTINEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOPOLSKI
utterances.text: While we're dealing with individuals who may or may not have been in Lapusnik at the time, Mr. Lehtinen, may I ask you this: Are you aware of the existence of a village doctor in Lapusnik in the summer, spring and summer of 1998?

utterances.speaker: OLE LEHTINEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have received information about a doctor being in Lapusnik at this time.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOPOLSKI
utterances.text: Have you traced him or her?

utterances.speaker: OLE LEHTINEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not me personally, but he's been met, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOPOLSKI
utterances.text: He's been met. Has he or she -- it's a he?

utterances.speaker: OLE LEHTINEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOPOLSKI
utterances.text: Has he made a statement?

utterances.speaker: OLE LEHTINEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOPOLSKI
utterances.text: Does it follow from the answers you've just given Their Honours his identity is known?

utterances.speaker: OLE LEHTINEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have to think about this.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOPOLSKI
utterances.text: Sorry.

utterances.speaker: OLE LEHTINEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: The -- we have found out one -- an identity of one doctor that was supposed to be in Lapusnik at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOPOLSKI
utterances.text: He's been seen, spoken to, but has not provided a statement. Is that the position?

utterances.speaker: OLE LEHTINEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is correct. And it was his own choice not to provide a statement.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOPOLSKI
utterances.text: Yes. Do you recollect his name?

utterances.speaker: OLE LEHTINEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not at this moment.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOPOLSKI
utterances.text: You don't.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Mr. Topolski, I'm sorry to interrupt. We've found the --

utterances.speaker: MR. TOPOLSKI
utterances.text: Oh, that's very kind.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: I believe the clip you were referring to.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOPOLSKI
utterances.text: Thank you. Right. Can we go back to what Musliu may have looked like at the time we're dealing with, please, and show this clip.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOPOLSKI
utterances.text: Do you have it?

utterances.speaker: OLE LEHTINEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOPOLSKI
utterances.text: Do you see Mr. Limaj -- well, the person who it is suggested is Mr. Limaj. I don't know if it's disputed, that that's Mr. Limaj in the front there. Yes? Is that Mr. Limaj, to the right?

utterances.speaker: OLE LEHTINEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think so, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOPOLSKI
utterances.text: Right. Look at the short chap behind him. I suggest that's Isak Musliu.

utterances.speaker: OLE LEHTINEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: The one behind him on the left?

utterances.speaker: MR. TOPOLSKI
utterances.text: The behind him in the middle of him and the other gentleman in the different shape and colour of uniform. The third man in the line there. Yeah?

utterances.speaker: OLE LEHTINEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: From this picture I couldn't be sure.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOPOLSKI
utterances.text: You can't say?

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Do you want the clip played?

utterances.speaker: MR. TOPOLSKI
utterances.text: No, thank you. That's all.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOPOLSKI
utterances.text: There's another individual I want to ask you about, please. Can you go to tab 6. This is a witness called Qiriqi, Ramiz Qiriqi. We've touched upon his name earlier this afternoon in another context. This is the fourth page of one of the interviews with him, Mr. Lehtinen. I think you were present at the interviews with him. Yes, you were.

utterances.speaker: OLE LEHTINEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOPOLSKI
utterances.text: At page 1. "In our investigation," you tell him on this page, "you are considered a suspect. This duty investigation we've done so far, we've done a lot of work in this case, people are coming up in different statuses. Because of the information we had about you, we have decided to interview you and invite you as a suspect." Mr. Lehtinen, were you part of the decision-making process that designated people suspects?

utterances.speaker: OLE LEHTINEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I was part of it, but it would not have been my decision.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOPOLSKI
utterances.text: You would have had an input into the making of that decision, based upon material you gathered at that stage?

utterances.speaker: OLE LEHTINEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOPOLSKI
utterances.text: And he or she who starts out life as a suspect and then becomes a Prosecution witness in regard to that decision, are you part of that process?

utterances.speaker: OLE LEHTINEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, part of it.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOPOLSKI
utterances.text: In this same interview an allegation is made regarding the conduct of the KLA. And I want to use this interview as the opportunity of inviting you to deal with it. Could you go on, please, to page 28 of the interview itself, 9720 at the top, or if you prefer, tab 7. You're still interviewing Ramiz Qiriqi. And could you remind Their Honours what status Qiriqi had in the KLA at this stage.

utterances.speaker: OLE LEHTINEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the KLA?

utterances.speaker: MR. TOPOLSKI
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: OLE LEHTINEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: His status in the KLA?

utterances.speaker: MR. TOPOLSKI
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: OLE LEHTINEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: He was commander of a headquarters -- a KLA headquarters in the KLA.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOPOLSKI
utterances.text: An important figure?

utterances.speaker: OLE LEHTINEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOPOLSKI
utterances.text: I just want to ask you about what you're putting to him here, and the basis of it. "People" -- just over halfway down the page is a question from you. "Some people were talking about bringing money to the headquarters. One example is in" -- how do you pronounce that?

utterances.speaker: OLE LEHTINEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Kroimire.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOPOLSKI
utterances.text: "Kroimire, where you were a commander. Kind of security money, not being hurt or not being arrested even. On one hand some people talk about paying money for being able to continue as police officers with the Serb police even during the war. People had a business, say, a shop or something to be able to sell things to Serbs. And by paying money to the local" -- could you then turn the page, because it repeats itself but the sense of it reads on -- "to the local KLA commander," top of the next page. "They were secured and not touched. The other part of the story is you could pay the KLA to arrest someone or maybe hurt someone. Have you ever heard about this? "A. It's the first time I hear about this kind of thing." Mr. Lehtinen, was that series of questions or rather propositions put to Ramiz Qiriqi, based on evidence you had gathered?

utterances.speaker: OLE LEHTINEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOPOLSKI
utterances.text: Witnesses had spoken to investigators, had they, and spoken in a variety of ways, in effect, of paying protection money to the KLA; is that the case?

utterances.speaker: OLE LEHTINEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I can remember one witness mentioning this.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOPOLSKI
utterances.text: One witness. More than one?

utterances.speaker: OLE LEHTINEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I recall one witness at this stage that has given a statement concerning this.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOPOLSKI
utterances.text: Are you able to identify who that is from memory?

utterances.speaker: OLE LEHTINEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, but he is a protected witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOPOLSKI
utterances.text: He is a protected witness?

utterances.speaker: OLE LEHTINEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOPOLSKI
utterances.text: I wonder if you would be good enough, with His Honour's leave, to give us his name on a piece of paper. Or do you happen to remember the number he's known by? No. Too much to ask on a Friday evening.

utterances.speaker: OLE LEHTINEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Witness complies]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOPOLSKI
utterances.text: Still under the heading of specific individuals, Mr. Lehtinen, may I ask you one or two questions about Jakup Krasniqi. We've been hearing much of his utterances in the communiques. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: OLE LEHTINEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOPOLSKI
utterances.text: Let's just look, if we may, at what he himself was telling you or your colleagues about his own communiques and utterances. Tab 10, please. You'll forgive me, Mr. Lehtinen, I think it's right that you weren't present here, but this is -- these are, rather, investigator's notes of meeting with Mr. Jakup Krasniqi. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: OLE LEHTINEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOPOLSKI
utterances.text: And I wonder if I could draw yours and others' attention to paragraphs 20 to 26 of that document. Mr. Krasniqi is being asked in this -- and you've seen these notes before, haven't you, Mr. Lehtinen?

utterances.speaker: OLE LEHTINEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I have.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOPOLSKI
utterances.text: Mr. Krasniqi is being asked in this interview, is he not, a good deal of questions regarding these various communiques and so on, press reports?

utterances.speaker: OLE LEHTINEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOPOLSKI
utterances.text: He talks here about the role of propaganda. Yes?

utterances.speaker: OLE LEHTINEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOPOLSKI
utterances.text: I have no doubt, Mr. Lehtinen, that you factored that in. You took into account, did you, in your open, honest, and objective search for the truth in this case the role of propaganda as far as these communiques were concerned. Would that be right?

utterances.speaker: OLE LEHTINEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that was considered.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOPOLSKI
utterances.text: The role of misinformation, did you consider that?

utterances.speaker: OLE LEHTINEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOPOLSKI
utterances.text: The role of disinformation, did you consider that?

utterances.speaker: OLE LEHTINEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOPOLSKI
utterances.text: The language that Krasniqi is using that you were highlighting through Mr. Whiting was designed to be put in the public domain, was it not, through communiques, through the press?

utterances.speaker: OLE LEHTINEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOPOLSKI
utterances.text: And to be put in the public domain in the press at a time of -- I'll just pause for a minute.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Please carry on, Mr. Topolski, I was not wanting to interrupt you.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOPOLSKI
utterances.text: No, not at all. I didn't want to distract Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOPOLSKI
utterances.text: Put into the press and into the public domain at a time, obviously, of war.

utterances.speaker: OLE LEHTINEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOPOLSKI
utterances.text: Can I move on from individuals to another topic, please, and that is the military police. We, I imagine, will hear much of that organisation, Mr. Lehtinen, in the trial. Can we see if we can establish through the words of witnesses in this bundle exactly what the functions of the military police were. Can we begin with Mr. Qiriqi again. Can you go to tab 8 now.

utterances.speaker: OLE LEHTINEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have the right.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOPOLSKI
utterances.text: Thank you. Tab 8, other part of a Qiriqi interview where you are dealing with the military police. You ask him near the top of the page: "Could we then speak a little about the military police in the KLA? In the beginning was battalion policy -- who was supposed to take orders from me? Very soon this competence was transferred," says Mr. Qiriqi, "to the brigade command." Over the page here he really starts to deal, Mr. Lehtinen, with what they were to do, the military police. Over the page, page 21 of this part of the interview, 9659 at the top. Does he say this: "They were supposed to keep an eye on army behaviour, how the army behaved with the civilians. They were supposed to check the army as well as civilian population in the area they were assigned to." And a little further down the page: "Even then there were rumours military police were more powerful than battalion commanders themselves, yet they had the power to detain or arrest even if I went against the rules." And a little later on that page: "They were not on the front line, but whenever there was fighting they were present there." And you ask him over the page did he know who was the commander of the military police and he gives a first name, Nexhmedin. When Qiriqi speaks about the function of the military police there, Mr. Lehtinen, do you agree with him as you understood it in 1998?

utterances.speaker: OLE LEHTINEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: The situation with the military police in the summer of 1998 is not very clear to me, and different witnesses describe it in a different way. But this is one way of describing it.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOPOLSKI
utterances.text: One way. Did it develop as we go through 1998, the role and duties of the military police, as you understood it?

utterances.speaker: OLE LEHTINEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it clearly developed.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOPOLSKI
utterances.text: Did it seem to have more of a function of monitoring army or civilians or both as the year developed of 1998?

utterances.speaker: OLE LEHTINEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would -- my understanding is that the emphasis was on the army.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOPOLSKI
utterances.text: On the army?

utterances.speaker: OLE LEHTINEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOPOLSKI
utterances.text: Of course the client I represent was a member of the military police, was he not?

utterances.speaker: OLE LEHTINEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOPOLSKI
utterances.text: Have your investigations thrown up or revealed to you that there were parts of Kosovo where training was set up for military police officers?

utterances.speaker: OLE LEHTINEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot recall now.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOPOLSKI
utterances.text: You cannot recall. Well, I think you can confirm though is that they were people who were eventually to wear black uniforms. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: OLE LEHTINEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOPOLSKI
utterances.text: Is it your understanding, as I suggest was the case, Mr. Lehtinen, that some people wore black uniforms prior -- before -- the establishing of the military police. Do you agree?

utterances.speaker: OLE LEHTINEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOPOLSKI
utterances.text: There was a history, was there not, in Kosovo in the years preceding 1998 of, I suggest, a huge percentage of the population being detained by Serb authorities. Many people were detained, were they not --

utterances.speaker: OLE LEHTINEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOPOLSKI
utterances.text: -- over the years. The reputation of the Serb police and other authorities was not a good one among Kosovar Albanians, was it, Mr. Lehtinen?

utterances.speaker: OLE LEHTINEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOPOLSKI
utterances.text: They were reviled, hated, and feared in equal measure, I suggest. Would that be fair?

utterances.speaker: OLE LEHTINEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOPOLSKI
utterances.text: And to this day, a Kosovar Albanian person's response to a person in uniform may be affected by that experience from the mid- to late-1980s. Would you agree? Or can't you say? It's left a mark, you would agree?

utterances.speaker: OLE LEHTINEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yeah, I'll agree.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOPOLSKI
utterances.text: I'll settle for that. Let's move on then to the subject of Serbs and Serb networks. From your investigations, from your work, from your knowledge of the situation in 1998, there were Serb infiltrators into the KLA, were there not?

utterances.speaker: OLE LEHTINEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Of Serb ethnicity? Is that your question? Are you asking me as to persons who were of Serb ethnicity in the KLA?

utterances.speaker: MR. TOPOLSKI
utterances.text: And people put into the KLA by the Serb authorities as infiltrators, as informants.

utterances.speaker: OLE LEHTINEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have no information about Serbs being infiltrated into the KLA.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOPOLSKI
utterances.text: Who was infiltrated into the KLA? Do you have knowledge of that?

utterances.speaker: OLE LEHTINEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have heard indications about ethnic Albanians working for the Serbs for information.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOPOLSKI
utterances.text: Right. As informants?

utterances.speaker: OLE LEHTINEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOPOLSKI
utterances.text: Do you distinguish in your own mind, Mr. Lehtinen, between an informant and an agent provocateur?

utterances.speaker: OLE LEHTINEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: The words at least, but I would need to have a clarification for the question.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOPOLSKI
utterances.text: An informant may be somebody who passes back information. An agent provocateur may be someone who provokes conduct and then informs upon the person who carries it out. Do you follow?

utterances.speaker: OLE LEHTINEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOPOLSKI
utterances.text: Are you aware of the latter being infiltrated into the KLA?

utterances.speaker: OLE LEHTINEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes, I am -- or I've heard about such.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOPOLSKI
utterances.text: In Serb authorities in the shape of the Milosevic regime were conducting a war as they saw it, were they not, against the KLA?

utterances.speaker: OLE LEHTINEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOPOLSKI
utterances.text: They considered them to be insurgents, revolutionaries, did they not?

utterances.speaker: OLE LEHTINEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOPOLSKI
utterances.text: Nom de guerre. Can I ask you about that?

utterances.speaker: OLE LEHTINEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOPOLSKI
utterances.text: Is it the case, Mr. Lehtinen, from you knowledge of the situation, that the use of noms de guerre were self-protective for the KLA. Do you understand me?

utterances.speaker: OLE LEHTINEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I understand. And in many cases it's explained as self-protected for the person using the name.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOPOLSKI
utterances.text: Yes. The fear was that if the real identity of the particular KLA member got out and got to the wrong person, that could have literally life-or-death consequences for that person's family back home. That was the fear, wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: OLE LEHTINEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOPOLSKI
utterances.text: So we are not to misinterpret or misunderstand the use of the noms de guerre, are we. It's not people being macho all over the place, it's people protecting themselves?

utterances.speaker: OLE LEHTINEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: In many cases, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOPOLSKI
utterances.text: In many cases. Can I move on from that to deal with another topic, and that is, if you like, the approach of witnesses and their responses to you and your investigating colleagues. Do you agree, Mr. Lehtinen, that in terms of the investigation for the most part you were dealing -- in terms of the civilians I mean -- with people from very much a rural setting?

utterances.speaker: OLE LEHTINEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOPOLSKI
utterances.text: Country people?

utterances.speaker: OLE LEHTINEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOPOLSKI
utterances.text: I think we heard this afternoon a reference to a document of somebody speaking about blood revenge. That is a feature, isn't it, of Albanian society?

utterances.speaker: OLE LEHTINEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOPOLSKI
utterances.text: I think the person I'm thinking of - and you may know who I'm talking about - says They must have made it up about me because there is some blood revenge between me and the other person. Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: OLE LEHTINEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yeah, it could be understood that way.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOPOLSKI
utterances.text: Apart from the settling of old scores and blood revenge, you came across, did you not, Mr. Lehtinen, people having political reasons for making false allegations?

utterances.speaker: OLE LEHTINEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. This could have been brought up as one reason.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOPOLSKI
utterances.text: I don't represent him, but it would be particularly appropriate, wouldn't it, in relation, potentially, to the case of Mr. Fatmir Limaj who was actively political at the time, was he not?

utterances.speaker: OLE LEHTINEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOPOLSKI
utterances.text: You would have to take that into account, would you not, when you were conducting your investigation?

utterances.speaker: OLE LEHTINEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOPOLSKI
utterances.text: Did you?

utterances.speaker: OLE LEHTINEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOPOLSKI
utterances.text: Albanian reaction to investigators borne of the same problems we were talking about a minute ago, treatment by the Serbs over the years. Did that present a difficulty? People reacting to investigators coming knocking at their door?

utterances.speaker: OLE LEHTINEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: It could affect in a way, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOPOLSKI
utterances.text: It could affect in a way, yes. Meaning?

utterances.speaker: OLE LEHTINEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Can I have the question again, sorry, because --

utterances.speaker: MR. TOPOLSKI
utterances.text: Yeah. Let's be specific about it, if I may. People show up at the front door of somebody in a rural village community in Kosovo and say: We're from the ICTY and we're investigating war crimes. Do you take into account the possibility that these people may feel threatened by the presence of people they would regard as more police officers?

utterances.speaker: OLE LEHTINEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOPOLSKI
utterances.text: Did they feel threatened, some of them, by the presence of police officers?

utterances.speaker: OLE LEHTINEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is possible, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOPOLSKI
utterances.text: Well, Mr. Lehtinen, did you have to reassure anybody, Don't be frightened, we're not going to be like the Serbs were, we're going to treat you decently and speak to you nicely. Did you have to say that sort of thing?

utterances.speaker: OLE LEHTINEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't use those words.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOPOLSKI
utterances.text: Of course not.

utterances.speaker: OLE LEHTINEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: But -- on some occasions you could see the fear.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOPOLSKI
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: OLE LEHTINEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOPOLSKI
utterances.text: Your Honour, I want to move on to some of the evidence that Mr. Lehtinen has been giving us which I don't think I could conclude in three minutes. I wonder whether --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: A nod is as good as a wink or something or other, Mr. Topolski, at this hour.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOPOLSKI
utterances.text: Well, could I ask Your Honour to take pity on an advocate at 7.00 on a Friday evening.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: I think that's for all of us. We'll adjourn now for the weekend. We'll resume on Monday morning at 9.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Monday, the 22nd day of November, 2004, at 9.00 a.m.

procedural_notes.text: --- Whereupon the hearing adjourned at 6.59 p.m.,
